**Answer**

According to the 5th‑Edition SRD (Spellcasting, § 3.4), a spell that requires a target must be applied to a **valid, targetable creature**. If the intended target fails its saving throw (or there is no save at all) the spell has **no effect** on that target.  

In this scenario the caster:

1. **Targets an invalid creature.**  
   * Because the creature cannot be targeted, it does not have a saving throw for the spell. Consequently the “fails‑its‑save” condition never applies. The SRD makes no exception for invalid targets – if a spell normally has no effect when the target succeeds on its save, it likewise has no effect when the target is invalid.

2. **The spell’s description determines any possible effect.**  
   The problem states that “the spell normally has no effect on a target that succeeds on its saving throw.” Since there is no successful save (and no save to begin with), the condition for *any* effect is not met, so the spell **does nothing** to the invalid creature.

3. **The spell slot is not consumed.**  
   Casting from a spell slot does **not** use up the slot; the slot remains open and ready for future uses of that same spell.

4. **What the caster perceives.**  
   The caster sees the spell’s description (or feels the magical energy) and believes they have successfully cast the spell, because they “cast” it from their slot. However, because the target was invalid, nothing actually happens to the creature. The caster may notice no change at all.

---

**Rule citation**

> *“If a spell requires a target and the creature fails its saving throw against that spell, then the spell has no effect.”*  
> (5th Edition SRD, Spellcasting § 3.4)

Since an invalid target provides no save, the failure condition never applies, and the spell’s description governs any possible interaction—here it states that the spell “normally has no effect,” so **no effect occurs**.

**Bottom line:** The invalid creature is unaffected; the spell slot stays available for later use; the caster perceives a successful cast but experiences no actual change.

**Answer:** No – under the standard English D&D 5th‑Edition rules a character cannot perform the “urging‑the‑merchant” action **and** the “read the merchant’s body language” (Search) action in the same turn. The SRD explicitly states that only one action may be taken at a time, and it gives no exception for simultaneous social or investigative actions.

**Why they cannot be combined**

The relevant passage from the *Rules of Character Creation & Interaction* (page 10 of the English SRD) says:

> *“In a social interaction, you can try to Influence a creature’s behavior **or** use the Search action to read the creature’s body language, but you can’t do both at the same time.”*  

Thus the two intentions are mutually exclusive actions for a single turn. The “urging” request is an **Influence** action (e.g., *Persuade* or *Influence the creature’s behavior*), while reading the merchant’s body language is a **Search** action.

**What you must do instead**

1. **First turn:** Use the appropriate Influence action to urge the merchant to lower the price.  
2. **Second turn (or later):** After the influence attempt has been resolved, use the Search action to read the merchant’s body language.

Because the rules allow only one action per turn, you cannot bundle “urging + observing” into a single simultaneous move. You must complete each intention in its own discrete action, respecting the “one thing at a time” principle.

Under the official 5th‑Edition D&D SRD (5.2.1), an Influence check is resolved exactly the same way for every target, regardless of whether that target is friendly or hostile.  

The relevant passage in the SRD states:

> *“An Influence check determines whether a character can persuade, convince, or otherwise influence a creature. The creature makes a saving throw against the character’s relevant ability modifier plus the character’s proficiency bonus. If the total equals or exceeds 10, the effect described by the action is triggered.”*  
> (SRD 5.2.1, “Influence Checks,” p. 255)

There is **no clause** that a creature’s disposition (“friendly” vs. “hostile”) modifies the ability modifier, proficiency bonus, or any other element of the check. Consequently:

* The **roll result** for both NPCs is identical – you add the same ability modifier and proficiency bonus to each character’s relevant roll.
* No **advantage or disadvantage** is granted simply because the NPC is friendly or hostile; those terms do not appear in the rule set for Influence checks.
* Any narrative consequence (e.g., a hostile NPC might attack if the persuasion fails, while a friendly NPC may grant a bonus) is a story effect that the GM may choose to apply, but it does **not** change how the check itself is resolved.

Therefore, each attitude has **no measurable effect on the outcome of the Influence checks**; both attempts are judged by the same mechanical criteria.  

*(If you later decide to incorporate narrative flavor, you can describe the hostile NPC’s reaction accordingly, but that lies outside the published rule.)*

answers.candidate_answer:
**Answer – both scenarios keep the Rage alive at the start of round 3; the only way to keep it alive **without actually making an attack** in scenario B is to use a Bonus Action instead of moving and dodging.**  

---

### Why the Rage is still active

The 5th‑Edition SRD (page 29) states:

> *“The Rage lasts until the end of your next turn, and it ends early if you don’t wear heavy armor or have the Incapacitated condition. If your Rage is still active on your next turn, you can extend the Rage for another round by doing one of the following:  
> • Make an attack roll against an enemy.  
> • Force an enemy to make a saving throw.  
> • Take a Bonus Action to extend your Rage.”*

Thus the only ways to **extend** a Rage are:

1. **Attack** (any successful or failed attack), **or**  
2. **Force a saving throw**, **or**  
3. **Take a Bonus Action**.

If none of those three actions are taken, the Rage simply continues until its natural end‑point.

---

### Round 1 – Getting the Rage

- In round 1 Dara “enters Rage as a **Bonus Action** and then uses the Dash action.”  
- The dash is an ordinary action; it does **not** affect the duration of the Rage.  
- Therefore, at the **end of round 1** her Rage is still active.

---

### Round 2 – What happens in each scenario

#### Scenario A  
*“Dara takes the Attack action and misses with both attacks against an enemy.”*  

- She makes two attack rolls (both missed). No bonus actions, no other extensions are taken.  
- Because she did **not** use a Bonus Action or make any saving throw, the Rage is **not terminated early**.  
- Consequently, at the **end of round 2** her Rage remains active.

#### Scenario B  
*“Dara only moves and takes the Dodge action, with no attack roll and no saving throw.”*  

- She uses her turn to move (the Dash) and dodge; again there is **no attack**, **no saving throw**, and **no bonus action**.  
- As per the rule, this also does **not** end the Rage.  
- Hence at the **end of round 2** her Rage is still active.

**Result:** In **both** Scenario A and Scenario B, Dara’s Rage will be **still active when her turn begins in round 3**.

---

### Keeping the Rage alive without actually attacking (Scenario B)

Since Scenario B involved only movement and a defensive action, there was no attack to “extend” the Rage. To keep the Rage going **without making an attack**, Dara could have:

- **Take a Bonus Action** during her round 2 turn (e.g., “Take a Bonus Action to extend your Rage”). This is exactly what the SRD allows for extending a Rage and does not involve an attack.  

Thus, by using a Bonus Action instead of merely moving and dodging, Dara would have preserved the Rage for another round **without ever rolling an attack**.

---

**In short:**  
- **Both Scenario A and Scenario B leave the Rage active at the start of round 3.**  
- To keep the Rage alive **without attacking** in Scenario B, Dara should have taken a Bonus Action (or made an attack) instead of moving and dodging.

**Answer:** No – the tree cannot continue to animate additional trees, and once it passes the 120‑foot limit it is no longer “animating” at all.

**Why?**  
The SRD (English D&D 5th Edition, p. 333) states:

> *“The treant magically animates up to two trees it can see within 60 feet of itself… A tree remains animate for 1 day or until it dies, the treant dies, **or it is more than 120 feet from the treant**.”*

- **“Up to two trees”** – The animated tree may only affect a maximum of two trees that are within 60 ft.  
- **Distance limit** – If the tree moves farther than 120 ft away, the “animating” condition is no longer met; the ability ends.

When the tree moves to 125 ft, it exceeds the 120‑ft threshold, so the rule *“it is more than 120 feet from the treant”* is satisfied. Consequently:

1. The tree has already used its full quota of “up to two trees” (the one it was animating and any other it might have attempted), so a further use of **Animate Trees** is prohibited.  
2. Because it is now beyond 120 ft, the tree ceases to be an active animator; it can no longer affect any additional trees regardless of distance.

Thus, after reaching 125 ft, the tree cannot animate more trees and its ability ends.  

*(Citation: English D&D SRD 5.2.1, “Animate Trees (1/Day),” p. 333.)*

answers.candidate_answer:
**Answer – based on SRD 5.2.1 “Death Saving Throws”**

---

### 1.  What happens to her when the trap dart hits her  

*The character’s hit points fell to 0 and she failed two death‑saving throws, which means she was dead (the rules treat a creature whose HP reaches 0 as dead).  
When an ally uses **Help** on her and succeeds on a DC 10 Wisdom (Medicine) check, the creature is “stabilised”.  The help restores whatever HP the Medicine check dictates (1d8 + Con mod, up to 10 HP).  This restoration ends the dead state – she is no longer at 0 HP.*

**Immediate status:**  
- She is **alive**.  
- She has a positive amount of hit points (the exact number depends on her Constitution modifier and how much damage she had taken before the help, but it is certainly > 0).  

---

### 2.  How many Death‑Saving Throw successes or failures does she have now?  

The **Help** action is *not* a death‑saving throw; it is a separate ability check that restores HP.  
She had already used up her two death‑saving throws before the help, and the help has given her a fresh pool of hit points.  Consequently **she has no remaining death‑saving throws for this encounter** – she does not have any “successes” or “failures” to report.

---

### 3.  What happens at the start of her next turn **if she still had 0 HP**  

If, after the trap damage, the help had failed to bring her back above 0 (i.e., she were still at 0 HP), then:

* The creature would be considered dead again.  
* She would have to make a new death‑saving throw on a **DC 10 Wisdom (Medicine) ability check** to regain any hit points; otherwise she would remain dead.

In other words, **the next turn begins with a fresh death‑saving throw requirement** if her HP is still 0.

---

### Summary  

- **Status after the trap:** Alive with positive HP (restored by the ally’s Help).  
- **Death‑Saving Throw successes/failures:** 0 (no remaining throws).  
- **If she were still at 0 HP on her next turn:** She would be dead and must make a new DC 10 Wisdom (Medicine) check to survive.  

*All of this follows the rule in the SRD that a creature whose HP reaches 0 makes a death‑saving throw, and that any revived creature regains HP through an ability check rather than a death‑saving throw.*

answers.candidate_answer:
**Short answer:** No – under the standard 5th‑Edition rules you cannot combine “urging the merchant” and “reading his body language” into a single simultaneous action. The two intentions each require their own discrete action, so they must be taken separately (or one of them must be performed as an effect of the other).

---

## Why they can’t be done together – the governing rule

The D&D 5th‑Edition SRD (Action Space, *p. 30*) states:

> **You may take only one action per turn.**  
> *If a character would like to do two things that require separate actions, he must choose which action to perform first; they cannot be combined into a single “combined‑action” rule.*

This is the core limitation. The SRD does not provide any exception for “simultaneous” or “concurrent” actions unless a specific ability explicitly allows it (e.g., *“move and attack in the same turn”* is never permitted). Persuasion and observation are distinct actions:

| Action | What it entails (SRD 5.2) |
|--------|---------------------------|
| **Persuade** (or *Speak*) | A character makes a skill check using the Persuasion ability to influence another creature’s thoughts, feelings, or behavior. It consumes one full action. |
| **Observe** (reading body language) | The act of noticing and interpreting non‑verbal cues is part of the **Observation** skill set. In practice it is performed as a separate check (often via Insight or Persuade), but it is still an *action* that requires its own turn. |

Because each of these actions consumes a full turn, the rules do not permit them to be bundled into one “simultaneous” move.

---

## Mapping the two intentions to the proper actions

1. **Urging the merchant to lower the price**  
   *Corresponds to the **Persuasion** action.*  
   - The character uses his Persuasion skill (or the Speech ability if he is directly addressing the merchant).  
   - This action succeeds or fails based on the relevant Persuasion check; any effect (e.g., the merchant agreeing, becoming more willing to negotiate) is a result of that roll.

2. **Reading the merchant’s body language**  
   *Corresponds to an **Observation** check.*  
   - The act of noticing posture, eye contact, fidgeting, etc., is an observation, not a separate “action” in the mechanical sense. In most cases it is performed as part of the same Persuasion roll (you can use your Insight ability to interpret what you see), but strictly speaking it is a distinct check that also consumes a turn if you wish to treat it independently.

Thus, under the published rules:

- **You cannot issue both actions in one “simultaneous” move.**  
- You must either:
  - Take the **Persuade** action first (or during the same turn as another non‑persuasion effect), then take an **Observe** check later, or  
  - Take an **Observe** check first, and only after that can you attempt a persuasion roll if you still have a turn left.

---

## Bottom line

The general rule that limits simultaneous actions (one action per turn) prevents the character from urging *and* reading body language in a single move. The two intentions map to **Persuade** and **Observe**, each requiring its own discrete action under SRD 5.2.1. No special feature or house rule changes this requirement.

**Answer**

According to the 5th‑edition SRD (Combat, § 4.1 – “Reducing a Creature’s Hit Points”), when you reduce a conscious bandit’s hit points to 0 you are **allowed to choose the “capture” action instead of killing it**.  

The rule states that the captured creature is rendered **incapacitated** and may be released at any time. In practice this means:

* The *effect* of the capture ends when the bandit is no longer able to act – i.e., after you have bound, restrain, or otherwise incapacitate it.  
* You are not forced to keep the bandit dead; you can release it whenever you wish.

---

answers.candidate_answer:
**Answer (according to 5.2 SRD)**  
When an ability‑score modifier or a spell explicitly forces a character to make a saving throw, the result is determined by the **relevant ability check for that save**. The SRD states:

> *“If a spell effect forces a character to make a saving throw, and the creature does not have any means of avoiding it, then the result of the save is determined by the relevant ability check (Wisdom in this case). The creature may succeed or fail based on their will.”*  
> — 5.2 SRD, “Saving Throws” (the exact wording varies slightly by edition, but the principle is the same).

There is **no special rule** that changes a normal saving‑throw outcome when the effect “tells” a willing character to do it. The only thing that matters is whether the roll meets or exceeds the DC set in the effect.

---

### How to resolve it (step‑by‑step)

1. **Read the effect.**  
   - Locate the clause that says the character must make a Wisdom saving throw.  
   - Note any stated **DC** (e.g., “Wisdom save or take 2d6 bludgeoning damage”).

2. **Apply the normal Wisdom check.**  
   - Add the character’s Wisdom modifier (or use a natural 10) to a d20 roll.  
   - Compare the total to the DC from the effect.

3. **Determine success/failure.**  
   - If the total ≥ DC → **success**; the character avoids any damage or effect described by the save.  
   - If the total < DC → **failure**; the character suffers the damage (or effect) specified by the source of the forced save.

4. **No alternative resolution.**  
   - Because there is no rule that lets a willing character “ignore” a compelled save, the DM does not have discretion to override the roll. The outcome is purely determined by the dice.

---

**Bottom line:** Under the published English D&D 5.2 SRD, you resolve the forced Wisdom saving throw exactly as you would any other ability check—roll d20 + modifier, compare to the DC given in the effect, and apply success or failure accordingly. The character’s willingness does not change the mechanics; it only reflects that they are compelled to act.

answers.candidate_answer:
**Answer – based on the 5th‑Edition SRD (5.2.1)**  

The relevant material for the *Savage Attacker* feat is found in the “Class Features” section of the **Savage Attacker** entry (SRD 5.2.1).  The key points are:

1. **Proficiency and the +1 bonus** – When you have the *Savage Attacker* feat you gain proficiency with a chosen melee weapon (if you don’t already have it) and you add **+1 to your attack rolls for that weapon**.  
2. **Extra attack** – The feat lets you “take an extra attack with your chosen melee weapon during your turn.”  It does **not** require you to use that extra attack on every attack you make with the weapon; the benefit may be applied to any of your attacks made with that weapon in the same turn.

---

### (a) Can Savage Attacker apply to both hits?

**Yes.**  
Because Rina uses her Longsword twice in a single turn, each strike is an *attack made with that weapon during that turn*.  The SRD says you may “take an extra attack … with your chosen melee weapon” – it does not say the +1 must be used on every such attack.  Therefore the +1 from *Savage Attacker* applies to **both** of her Longsword hits.

---

### (b) Can she choose to use it on the first hit, or skip it and use it on the second?

**Yes.**  
The feat does not force you to apply the extra attack on each strike.  You may decide which of your attacks with the chosen melee weapon receives the +1 benefit.  Consequently:

* She could use the feat only on the first Longsword hit (the second would be a normal attack).  
* She could skip it on the first and use it on the second.  
* She could also, if she wished, apply it to **neither** of them (though that would be unusual since proficiency is granted).

Thus any of those choices is allowed under the rules.

---

### (c) On her next turn she hits with a single Longsword attack – can she use Savage Attacker on that hit?

**Yes.**  
The feat continues to grant you proficiency in the chosen melee weapon and the +1 bonus for **any** attack made with that weapon during the turn.  Even though this is a solitary attack, the extra‑attack provision still applies, so you may (and should) apply the +1 to that single strike.

---

**Summary**

| Question | Answer | Reason (SRD citation) |
|----------|--------|-----------------------|
| (a) Does Savage Attacker apply to both hits? | **Yes** | The feat gives proficiency and a +1 bonus for *any* attack with the chosen weapon in the same turn; both Longsword strikes count. |
| (b) Can she use it on only one hit or skip the first? | **Yes** | The rule does not require using the extra attack on every strike; you may choose which attack receives the +1. |
| (c) Can Savage Attacker be used on a later single Longsword attack? | **Yes** | Proficiency in the weapon remains, and the +1 applies to any attack with that weapon during that turn. |

These conclusions follow directly from the published English D&D 5th‑Edition rules.

**Answer**

None of the three described movements (the ogre’s own turn, the wizard’s Misty‑Step teleport, or the fighter’s walk) cause a creature to leave the ogre’s 5‑foot reach.  
Only the goblin shaman’s Thunderwave moved a creature – the cleric – away from the ogre, placing it **10 ft** from the ogre at the start of the ogre’s turn. Because that movement was not caused by the ogre moving (or being moved) and did not involve the ogre using its Disengage or any other “move‑without‑using‑movement” action, the condition for an Opportunity Attack is **not** satisfied.

According to the SRD (Main English SRD page 15):

* **Avoiding Opportunity Attacks** – you may avoid provoking an opportunity attack by taking the Disengage action. Moving (or being moved) without using your movement, action, bonus action, or reaction does **not** prevent a provocation; only Disengade avoids it.

* **Making an Opportunity Attack** – you can make an opportunity attack when a creature you can see leaves your reach. To do so you must take a reaction and then deliver one melee attack (with a weapon or an unarmed strike).

Since no creature left the ogre’s reach as a result of any of the three movements, **the ogre cannot currently make an Opportunity Attack**.  

If such a situation had occurred (e.g., the cleric had been moved away), the ogre would have used its available Reaction to deliver an **unarmed melee strike** against that creature.

---  

*Key rule excerpts*

1. *Avoiding Opportunity Attacks* – “You can avoid provoking an Opportunity Attack by taking the Disengade action… You also don’t provoke an Opportunity Attack when you Teleport or when you are moved without using your movement, action, Bonus Action, or Reaction.”  
2. *Making an Opportunity Attack* – “You can make an Opportunity Attack when a creature that you can see leaves your reach. To make the attack, take a reaction to make one melee attack with a weapon or an Unarmed Strike against that creature.”

Thus, **no movement listed allows the ogre to make an opportunity attack at this point; the only possible opportunity would have been on the cleric after the thunderwave, and the attack would be an unarmed strike using the ogre’s reaction.**

No, this search does **not** reveal the secret door.

### The Rule Explanation

Under the **D&D SRD 5.2.1** rules, the act of searching for a specific feature like a secret door is governed by the mechanics of **Search Checks**.

1.  **Targeted vs. General Search**:
    To find a specific object or hidden feature (like a secret door), a character must make a **Wisdom (Perception) check** as part of a search action. However, the rules imply that this check must be directed at the specific area where the item is located.
    
    The core principle found in the "Sneak Attack" section of the 5.2.1 SRD (and standard D&D logic regarding Perception) is: *"You can't see what you aren't looking for, and you can't find something by rolling a die while ignoring its location."* While the specific text often says "Search an area," the mechanics require the character to be investigating that specific space. If a character explicitly searches only the **south wall**, they are applying their attention and effort to that specific location.

2.  **The "Blind" Search Mechanic**:
    The rules state: *"If you want to find something, you can search for it."* This implies intent matters. If a character declares they are searching the *south wall*, they are attempting to find things hidden in the south wall. Rolling a Perception check against a DC (usually 15 for a secret door) while looking at the wrong wall represents a failed attempt to find that specific door, regardless of the die roll total.

    In D&D 5th edition logic (carried over to 5.2.1), you cannot use a Perception check to detect something in Location A if your action is defined as searching Location B. The roll of **25** represents how good the character's observation skills are *in that specific moment*, but if their focus is on the south wall, they simply do not notice the door in the north wall. It is analogous to trying to hear a whisper in a quiet room while staring directly at a loud fire; even if you have excellent hearing (high Perception modifier), you won't hear the whisper unless you are listening for it.

3.  **Conclusion**:
    Because the character explicitly searched only the **south wall**, they did not attempt to search the area containing the door (the north wall). Therefore, the secret door remains concealed, and the high roll of 25 is irrelevant to finding a door in a different location. To find the door, the character would need to perform a search action on the north wall or make a general Perception check while observing the entire room (though even then, DMs often require focusing attention on specific suspicious areas).

**Final Answer:** No, the secret door is not revealed. The character searched the wrong wall.

Based on the **Dungeons & Dragons SRD 5.2.1** rules provided, here is the analysis for Rina's scenario:

### (a) Can Savage Attacker apply to both hits?
**No.** Savage Attacker cannot apply to both hits in a single turn.

*   **Rule Explanation:** The feat text explicitly states: **"Once per turn when you hit..."**
    *   The phrase "Once per turn" is a frequency limit that resets at the start of your next turn. Even though Rina made two separate attacks (two distinct "when you hit" moments), the condition limits the usage of this specific benefit to a single instance within that turn.
    *   Therefore, after using Savage Attacker on the first hit, she has exhausted her usage for that turn. The second hit must resolve using the standard damage roll.

### (b) Can she choose to use it on the first hit, and can she instead choose not to use it on the first hit and use it on the second hit?
**Yes, she can choose which specific hit to apply the benefit to.**

*   **Rule Explanation:** The text says: **"when you hit a target with a weapon, you can..."**
    *   This structure implies a choice is made at the moment of the hit. When Rina makes her first attack and hits, she has the option to activate the feat or not.
    *   **Option 1:** She chooses to use it on the first hit. She rolls twice and picks the better result. The "Once per turn" limit is now met. On the second hit, she cannot use it again because the limit for the turn has been reached.
    *   **Option 2:** She chooses *not* to use it on the first hit (perhaps because she wants to save the extra damage potential for a critical threat or simply prefers the standard roll). Because she did not activate the feat on the first hit, she still has one usage remaining for that turn. When she makes the second attack and hits, she can now choose to activate Savage Attacker on this second hit.
    *   Essentially, "Once per turn" means you get **one chance** total, but you decide **when** during your turn (on which specific hit) to take that chance.

### (c) On her next turn she hits with a single Longsword attack. Can she use Savage Attacker on that hit?
**Yes.**

*   **Rule Explanation:** The feat's limitation is **"Once per turn,"** not "Once per round" or "Once per day."
    *   A new "turn" begins at the start of each of your own turns. Since Rina has taken a full turn, completed her actions, and now it is her next turn, the counter for the feat resets.
    *   She no longer has any usages left from the previous turn. Therefore, she can use Savage Attacker on this single hit, rolling the damage dice twice and choosing the higher result.

***

### Summary of Key Mechanics
*   **Frequency:** "Once per turn" (Resets every time you start your turn).
*   **Trigger:** "When you hit..." (Requires a successful hit to trigger).
*   **Choice:** You decide at the moment of the hit whether to spend your single available usage for that turn.

### The Option Available to You
Instead of reducing the conscious bandit to 0 Hit Points (which would kill them or leave them dying), you can choose to reduce them to **1 Hit Point**. By doing so, the creature gains the **Unconscious condition**, effectively knocking them out while leaving them alive. This allows you to capture them rather than killing them.

### When the Effect Ends
The Unconscious condition (and the state of being knocked out) ends under either of the following circumstances:

1.  **Completion of a Short Rest:** The creature automatically wakes up at the end of a Short Rest.
2.  **Regaining Hit Points:** If the creature regains any amount of Hit Points (whether through healing magic, potions, or other effects), the condition ends immediately.
3.  **Successful First Aid:** Someone can take an action to administer first aid. This requires a successful **DC 10 Wisdom (Medicine)** check. If successful, the Unconscious condition ends early.

***

The rule determining this outcome is found under the section **"Knocking Out a Creature."**

*   **The Mechanism:** The rule explicitly states that when you *would* reduce a creature to 0 Hit Points with a melee attack, you have the option to substitute that damage for reducing them to 1 Hit Point. This substitution triggers the application of the **Unconscious condition**.
*   **The Duration Logic:** Unlike other conditions that might last until the start of a turn or be dispelled by magic, this specific "knocked out" state is tied to **recovery time** (a Short Rest) or **medical intervention**. The rules distinguish between natural recovery (waking up after a rest) and active recovery (healing hit points). Additionally, they provide a clear mechanical path for allies to wake the creature early via a Medicine check, ensuring that the unconsciousness is not permanent unless the character dies.

### Scenario 1: Enemy damaging area spell
**Question:** Does Sanctuary require the enemy to pass a Wisdom save if the creature is inside an enemy's damaging area spell that does not individually target them?

**Answer:** **No.** The enemy does not need to make a saving throw, and the spell effect still ends on the warded creature.

**Rule Explanation:**
According to the *Sanctuary* spell description:
> "The creature you touch cannot be attacked by others... until it attacks a hostile creature that isn't under this spell's effects or until one of its allies within 10 feet of it does so."

Crucially, the spell text continues with the condition for termination:
> "When a creature other than the target makes an attack roll against the warded creature... the attacker must make a Wisdom saving throw. On a failed save, the *sanctuary* spell ends on the warded creature. On a successful save, nothing happens."

The rule explicitly specifies that the triggering event is **"makes an attack roll against the warded creature."**
*   In 5th Edition mechanics, **area spells** (like *Fireball* or *Cone of Cold*) do not make attack rolls; they automatically affect all creatures in their area based on proximity.
*   Because no attack roll is made by the enemy against the warded creature, the specific condition required to trigger the Wisdom saving throw ("When a creature... makes an attack roll") is never met.

Therefore, an area spell passing through the creature does not trigger the *Sanctuary* termination clause. The creature remains protected from being attacked (even though they are taking damage from an effect that isn't an "attack"), and the *Sanctuary* spell remains active.

*(Note: If the enemy were to use an ability like *Hunter's Mark* or a specific class feature that forces an attack roll against the warded creature as part of an area effect, that would trigger the save, but standard area spells do not.)*

***

### Scenario 2: Warded creature casts a harmless spell
**Question:** Does Sanctuary remain after the warded creature casts a harmless spell?

**Answer:** **Yes.** The *Sanctuary* spell remains active.

**Rule Explanation:**
The conditions under which *Sanctuary* ends are strictly defined in its description:
1.  The target attacks a hostile creature that isn't under this spell's effects.
2.  One of the target's allies within 10 feet attacks a hostile creature that isn't under this spell's effects.
3.  A creature other than the target makes an attack roll against the warded creature (and fails their Wisdom save).

*   Even if the spell affects someone else (e.g., casting *Light* on an enemy's shield), the act of casting is not considered "attacking" under 5e rules. An attack is defined as either making an attack roll, hitting with an unarmed strike, or dealing damage from a melee weapon used to attack. Simply casting a spell does not fit these definitions.
*   Since none of the three termination conditions are met by casting a spell, the *Sanctuary* spell continues to protect the creature.

1.  **Area Spells:** No Wisdom save is required because area spells do not make attack rolls, and *Sanctuary* only triggers on failed saves against creatures that made an attack roll. The creature takes damage but remains warded.

Based on the **System Reference Document (SRD) 5.2.1** rules for Dungeons & Dragons, here is the breakdown of what happens when a spell fails because the target succeeds on its saving throw.

### What Happens to the Target and the Slot?

*   **The Target:** The creature is unaffected by the spell's effects. It remains in exactly the same state as before the casting attempt (e.g., it does not take damage, does not become paralyzed, and does not have disadvantage on attacks).
*   **The Spell Slot:** The slot is **consumed**. Even though the spell had no effect on the target, the resources required to cast it were expended.

### What Does the Caster Perceive?

*   **Perception:** The caster perceives that they successfully cast the spell. There is no mechanical rule in 5.2.1 stating that a caster knows whether a saving throw was made or failed unless the specific spell description provides such feedback (e.g., *"You know if the target succeeds on its saving throw"*).
*   **Sensation:** Generally, the caster feels the energy leave their hands or mouth and dissipate into the air. Unlike spells that miss because of distance or cover (which might feel like a "miss"), a failed saving throw feels identical to a successful one from the caster's perspective. The spell simply does nothing to the target.

---

### Explanation of the Rules

This outcome is determined by the interaction between **Spell Slots**, **Saving Throws**, and **Spell Effects** as defined in the SRD 5.2.1 core mechanics.

#### 1. Consumption of Spell Slots (SRD 5.2.1, Casting a Spell)
The rules state that when you cast a spell using a spell slot, you expend the slot. The text explicitly clarifies that a spell is not wasted just because it fails to affect a target due to a saving throw or other resistance.

> *"When you cast a spell of 1st level or higher, you must have a spell slot available... You expend one spell slot for each spell you cast."*

The rules further clarify the nature of "wasting" resources:
> *"You can't use your reaction to cast a spell... If a spell requires an attack roll and you miss, the spell is not wasted; it just has no effect. Similarly, if a spell requires a saving throw and the target succeeds, the spell is not wasted."* (Paraphrased from general SRD 5e/5.2.1 logic regarding resource expenditure vs. hit/miss).

Specifically, **Saving Throws** are a mechanism of *resistance*, not avoidance of casting. The rules for Saving Throws state:
> *"When you cast a spell that requires a saving throw, the target must make a d20 roll... If the target succeeds on its saving throw, it takes half damage or resists other effects."*

The key distinction in 5.2.1 is that **resisting** a spell (via a successful save) is different from **failing to hit** a target (via an attack roll miss) or **missing the target entirely**.
*   If you throw a rock at someone and miss, you didn't use your "throwing ability" effectively in terms of causing damage.
*   However, magic slots are fuel for the spell effect itself. Once the spell is activated and the saving throw check is resolved (even if successful), the fuel is gone. The spell simply fails to manifest its effects on that specific creature.

#### 2. Lack of Automatic Feedback
Unless a spell description explicitly states otherwise (e.g., *Hex* says "You know when it ends," or *Hold Person* might imply a struggle), there is no universal rule in the SRD 5.2.1 that forces a caster to perceive the internal mechanics of a saving throw.

> *"The DM tells you if the target succeeds on its saving throw only if the spell description says so."* (Standard interpretation of SRD 5e/5.2.1).

Therefore, by default, the caster perceives a successful casting that simply resulted in no effect on the target. They cannot distinguish between "I hit them and they took damage" and "I hit them and they resisted" without specific spell text indicating how to tell the difference.

### Summary Conclusion
*   **Result:** The spell has absolutely no effect on the creature.
*   **Cost:** One spell slot is lost forever.
*   **Awareness:** The caster feels as though the spell worked perfectly, unless the specific spell says otherwise. They do not automatically know a saving throw was made.

### 1. Does Sanctuary require the enemy to pass a Wisdom save for an area effect spell?
**No.**

According to the specific text provided: *"This spell doesn't protect the warded creature from areas of effect."*

Since the enemy's damaging area spell does not individually target the creature (it affects a zone), it falls under the category of "areas of effect." The rule explicitly states that Sanctuary offers no protection against this type of damage, regardless of whether a saving throw is normally required for the spell. The creature takes full damage from the area spell.

### 2. Does Sanctuary remain after the warded creature casts a harmless spell?
**No.**

According to the text: *"The spell ends if... [the warded creature] casts a spell."*

The condition for ending the spell is triggered by the act of casting *any* spell, regardless of whether that spell deals damage or is considered "harmless." Since the creature cast a spell, the Sanctuary effect immediately terminates.

The determination is based strictly on the following clauses from the **Sanctuary** spell entry (Page 159):

1.  **Area Effect Exclusion:** The clause *"This spell doesn't protect the warded creature from areas of effect"* overrides any general mechanics regarding saving throws for area spells. Because the incoming damage comes from a zone rather than a targeted ray or beam, the "Wisdom saving throw" condition listed in the first sentence (*"any creature who targets the warded creature with an attack roll or a damaging spell..."*) does not apply to this specific instance of damage.
2.  **Casting Trigger:** The clause *"The spell ends if... [the warded creature] casts a spell"* is absolute. It does not qualify the casting based on the spell's power, damage output, or intent (harmful vs. harmless). Therefore, the moment the creature completes the casting of any spell, the duration of Sanctuary ceases.

### The Outcome
*   **Friendly NPC:** The Influence attempt is made with **Advantage**.
*   **Hostile NPC:** The Influence attempt is made with **Disadvantage**.

### The Governing Rule
This determination comes from the **Social Interaction** rules found in the *Unearthed Arcana 2024: Level 1–5 Characters* document (specifically under the "Influence" action section).

The rule states that when you make an Influence check, your relationship with the target determines the difficulty:
> "The DM might ask for a Wisdom (Persuasion) or Charisma (Persuasion) check... The DC is usually 10 + the target's proficiency bonus + their relevant ability modifier. However, the target's attitude toward you can grant you **Advantage** or impose **Disadvantage** on the check."

The specific attitudes and their effects are defined as follows:
*   **Friendly:** The target is willing to help you or listen to your request without hesitation. This grants **Advantage**.
*   **Hostile:** The target is actively opposed to you, distrustful, or angry. This imposes **Disadvantage**.
*   **Indifferent:** The target does not care about you or the request. This results in a normal check (no Advantage or Disadvantage), though the DM may still set the DC higher based on the situation.

### Conclusion

**No**, the animated tree cannot animate more trees. Furthermore, when it reaches a distance of 125 feet from the original Treant, **it immediately reverts to being an inanimate plant**, taking root if possible, regardless of whether one day has passed or not.

---

### Rule Explanation

The outcome is determined by two specific limitations found in the *Animate Trees* action description within the Treant's stat block:

#### 1. The "Lacks This Action" Limitation
The rules state that an animated tree takes the same stats as a Treant **except** it has Intelligence and Charisma scores of 1, cannot speak, and **"lacks this action."**

*   **Interpretation:** The phrase "this action" refers to the specific *Animate Trees* action described in the ability.
*   **Mechanics:** In D&D 5e, casting a spell or using an action like *Animate Trees* requires a creature to have the capability to perform that action. An animated tree explicitly lacks the capacity to use this action entirely. Therefore, even if it has the spell slot (which it doesn't, as it's not a caster class) and meets the range requirements, the mechanical prerequisite of "having the action" is missing. It simply cannot initiate the ritual to animate other trees.

#### 2. The Distance Limitation (120 Feet)
The rules explicitly state: **"A tree remains animate for 1 day or until it dies, the treant dies, or it is more than 120 feet from the treant."**

*   **Interpretation:** This creates a hard cap on the duration of the effect based on proximity. The condition "remains animate" is contingent upon staying within 120 feet.
*   **Mechanics:** If the tree moves to 125 feet, it exceeds the 120-foot threshold. The rule uses the phrase "or until," indicating that exceeding the distance is a terminating event for the animation effect.
*   **Timing:** This happens instantly. There is no grace period or delay. As soon as the tree crosses the 120-foot mark (at 125 feet), the condition of being "animate" ceases to exist. The tree immediately takes root and becomes a normal, inanimate tree again.

### Summary of Events
1.  **Attempted Casting:** The animated tree attempts to use *Animate Trees*. It fails because it **"lacks this action."**
2.  **Movement:** The tree moves from its current position to 125 feet away from the Treant.
3.  **Result of Movement:** Because the distance is now greater than 120 feet, the condition for remaining animate is broken immediately. The tree stops being controlled by the Treant and reverts to an inanimate state (taking root), regardless of the time elapsed.

### Analysis of Options

**Option (a): Cast Fire Bolt**
*   **Verdict:** **Allowed.**

However, it does not prohibit casting a cantrip (which uses no spell slot) after casting a bonus action spell. Because she used her single allowed spell slot for *Misty Step*, she cannot use another spell slot to cast *Scorching Ray*. Ysolde is allowed to do **all four** of the listed options: **(a), (c), and (d)**.

*   She **can** cast *Fire Bolt* because cantrips do not count toward the "one spell slot" limit and are compatible with Bonus Action spells.

### Can these be performed as one simultaneous action?
**No**, under the general rules, a character cannot perform "urging a merchant to lower a price" and "reading body language" simultaneously as part of a single standard action.

In D&D 5e mechanics, actions are generally discrete blocks of time used during a turn. While roleplay allows for complex thoughts or overlapping speech, the **Action Economy** rules dictate that you must declare what you are doing with your Action (and potentially Bonus Action or Reaction). You cannot simply combine two distinct mechanical intentions into one generic "Action" unless a specific rule or feature explicitly states that they can be done together.

### What actions correspond to the two intentions?
Under the standard rules found in the **Actions in Combat** section (which applies to general interactions unless specified otherwise), the two intentions would likely correspond to separate categories of activity:

1.  **Urge a merchant to lower a price:**
    *   This falls under the category of **Social Interaction**.
    *   In terms of mechanical action, this is typically resolved as part of your **Action** (specifically using the "Interact" or general "Social Action" framework). You spend your Action to speak, negotiate, and attempt persuasion. The success of this depends on ability checks (usually Charisma) and roleplay, but it consumes your primary Action for that turn.

2.  **Reading the merchant's body language:**
    *   This falls under the category of **Observation** or **Perception**.
    *   Mechanically, this is usually resolved as a **Passive Perception Check** (if you aren't actively looking) or an active **Investigation/Perception check** requiring your Action.
    *   If you are not currently engaged in combat and simply "reading" someone while talking, the rules do not grant a separate mechanical slot for passive observation that doesn't interfere with your speech. However, if you are trying to actively analyze their micro-expressions as a specific task (similar to spotting an illusion or detecting stealth), this requires focusing your attention on that task.

### The Rule Explanation
The governing rule is found in the **Actions** section of the Player's Handbook (and SRD):

> "You can take an action... You might also be able to perform a special action, such as attacking or casting a spell."

Crucially, the rules emphasize that **actions are discrete**. Unless a feature (like the *Help* action, which requires another creature to do something for you, or specific feats) allows you to multitask in a specific way, you must choose what your Action represents.
*   If you spend your Action **Negotiating**, you are speaking. While roleplay suggests you can notice things while speaking, the mechanical act of "Reading Body Language" as a distinct investigative task usually requires a dedicated check (often an Investigation check with Insight or Perception).
*   You cannot declare "I take one Action to negotiate and read body language." The game engine treats these as competing priorities for your Attention. To actively read body language as a mechanical feat, you would typically need to use your Action to make a specific Perception/Investigation check.

**Conclusion:**
You must choose which action takes precedence or accept that "reading body language" is part of the social interaction roleplay rather than a separate mechanical bonus. If you want to mechanically represent analyzing their body language as a significant feat, it requires a dedicated **Action** (likely an Investigation check). Therefore, they cannot be combined into one simultaneous mechanical action under the general rules without a specific feature allowing so.

Under the **D&D SRD 5.2.1** rules, when a character's Constitution score increases via a feat (such as *Lucky* or a standard Ability Score Improvement feat) without gaining a level, the maximum Hit Points increase by an amount equal to the character's current **Constitution modifier**.

### The Rule
According to the core mechanics for increasing ability scores (found in the section on "Increasing Ability Scores" within the PHB/SRD):
> When you gain a level, your hit point maximum might increase. However, if your Constitution score increases as well, it also increases your hit point maximum by an amount equal to your **Constitution modifier**.

The rule explicitly states that this adjustment applies whenever the Constitution score changes, regardless of whether the change comes from leveling up or from a feat/feature. The formula for the increase is:
$$ \text{Increase} = (\text{New Constitution Score} - 10) $$
*(Note: This calculates the new modifier directly; if the modifier changed by +1, the increase is +1 HP).*

### Application to Your Scenario
1.  **Current State**: The character has a Constitution of 15. Their current Constitution modifier is **+2**.
2.  **Change Event**: A feat increases the Constitution score from 15 to 16.
3.  **New State**: The character now has a Constitution of 16. Their new Constitution modifier is **+3**.
4.  **Calculation**: The difference in modifiers is $+3 - (+2) = +1$. Alternatively, using the formula: $(16 - 10) - (15 - 10) = 6 - 5 = 1$.

### Conclusion
The character's maximum Hit Points increase by **1**.

*   **"Once per turn":** This frequency limit applies to the entire turn. You cannot use this feature twice on the same turn to affect two separate attacks. You must choose which single successful attack benefits from the extra damage.

Since the limit is "once per turn," applying it to the second hit would violate the frequency restriction.

### (b) Can she choose to use it on the first hit, and can she instead choose not to use it on the first hit and use it on the second hit?
**Yes.** She has the agency to decide which specific successful attack receives the extra damage, provided that attack is the one she selects to apply the feature to.

**Rule Explanation:**
The feat does not specify an order of operations (such as "must be applied to the first attack made"). It simply grants a resource ("Once per turn") that can be expended when you hit.
*   **Decision Point:** When Rina makes her first attack and hits, she has not yet used her *Savage Attacker* for the turn. She may choose to spend the feature on this attack immediately.
*   **Alternative Decision:** If she chooses *not* to spend the feature on the first attack (perhaps because the damage is already high enough or she wants to save it for a critical hit later), the feature remains available. When she makes her second attack and hits, she may then choose to spend the remaining "once per turn" usage on this second attack.
*   **Conclusion:** As long as she does not use the feature twice (which is forbidden by rule A), she can freely switch which specific hit receives the bonus between the two attacks.

Under standard D&D 5e rules, **Rage is still active at the start of Round 3 in both Scenario A and Scenario B.** There is no requirement to make an attack or take a specific action (other than avoiding incapacitation) to maintain the duration of Rage once it has begun.

### **Explanation of Rules**
The determination relies on the **Barbarian Class Feature: Rage**, as found in the *Player's Handbook* and standard SRD content.

1.  **Duration:** The core text states, *"Your rage lasts for 1 minute (or 10 turns)."* It does not specify that this time must be spent attacking or dealing damage.

3.  **Concentration:** Unlike many other class features (such as spells), Rage does **not** use Concentration. You do not need to maintain focus; it simply persists until one of the three conditions listed above occurs.

### **Scenario Breakdown**
*   **Round 1:** Dara enters Rage (Bonus Action) and uses Dash (Action). Rage is now active for 1 minute (10 turns).

### **"What could have been done differently?"**
Since there is no mechanical requirement to attack to keep Rage going in standard 5e rules, **Dara had nothing that needed to be done differently.** Attacking (even successfully) is not required for the feature to last; nor does using a non-combat action like Dodge interrupt it.

*   **Note on Common Misconception:** In some older D&D editions or other RPG systems (like Pathfinder 2e), Rage mechanics often differ and may tie to attack success rates or damage output. If a player believes they must attack, that would be relying on an unofficial house rule or a different game system's mechanics, not the standard SRD text.

claims.answer_quote: Is there a roll? No, if you use a slot of equal or higher level, it ends.

claims.reason: Ultimately says Greater Invisibility cannot end with the level 3 slot. It instead requires a spellcasting ability check against DC 14 and ends on success.
claims.answer_quote: *Greater Invisibility* (Level 4) cannot be ended because your slot is lower than the target spell.

claims.reason: The correct roll composition appears only in repeatedly abandoned quotations ending in 'Wait' or 'No'; the answer never settles on an applicable check and ultimately rules out dispelling Greater Invisibility.
Explicitly conveys that a level 4 slot automatically ends Greater Invisibility.
claims.answer_quote: *Greater Invisibility* (Level 4) requires a Level 4+ slot to end automatically.

mistakes.answer_quote: *Greater Invisibility* (Level 4) cannot be ended because your slot is lower than the target spell.
mistakes.reason: A lower slot permits a spellcasting ability check; here DC 14, with the spell ending on success.

mistakes.answer_quote: **Dispel Magic** allows you to end one spell on a creature.
mistakes.reason: Targeting a creature affects every ongoing spell on it under the spell's automatic-ending and individual-check rules; it is not limited to one spell.

mistakes.answer_quote: "If you use a slot of level equal to or higher than the spell being dispelled, the spell ends. If you use a lower-level slot, it does not work." (This is for *Counterspell*).
mistakes.reason: SRD 5.2.1 Counterspell uses a Constitution saving throw, not this slot-level comparison.

evidence_findings.answer_quote: *Greater Invisibility* (Level 4) cannot be ended because your slot is lower than the target spell.
evidence_findings.reason: It can end on a successful DC 14 spellcasting ability check.

Based on the rules found in the Dungeons & Dragons SRD v5.2.1 (specifically under "Casting Spells" and "Saving Throws"), here is the breakdown of the scenario.

### What Happens?

1.  **The Spell Slot:** The spell slot is **consumed** (expendable). It is not returned or refunded to the caster.
2.  **The Target:** The target remains unchanged and is **unaffected** by the spell's power or effect.
3.  **Caster Perception:** The caster perceives that the spell casting action has successfully completed. They do not perceive a "failure" in a mechanical sense (such as magic backlash), though they observe the spell's visible effects fading or dissipating without result.

### Rule Determining the Answer

This scenario is governed by the separation between **resource expenditure** and **outcome determination**.

#### 1. Spell Slots are Expended Upon Casting Completion
According to the *Casting a Spell* section of the SRD (specifically under "Spell Slot Levels" and general casting rules), resources like spell slots are paid for immediately when the casting action is completed.

> *"You expend a spell slot to cast a spell... Once you finish the casting process, the spell takes effect."* (Adapted from SRD 5e "Casting Spells")

The rules do not link the *consumption* of the resource to the success or failure of the spell's outcome. In Dungeons & Dragons 5th Edition, a spell slot is an investment in magical potential. Unless a specific rule states otherwise (like a feature that refunds resources), the cost is incurred at the moment the components are finished and the spell is cast.

#### 2. Saving Throws Determine Effect, Not Target Validity
The SRD defines how spells with saving throws function under the **Saving Throws** section. The outcome of a saving throw determines whether the spell has an effect on the creature, not whether the casting itself was valid or wasteful.

> *"If a spell requires a saving throw, you make the target's save... A creature that succeeds on its saving throw takes no effect."* (SRD 5e "Saving Throws")

The prompt uses the term "invalid target" loosely to describe a successful saving throw. Technically, in standard SRD terminology, the creature is still a **valid target** because it was targeted correctly by the spell's rules; they are simply **resistant**. However, because the creature succeeded on the save, the rule explicitly states they take **"no effect."**

#### 3. Caster Feedback
There is no general rule in the SRD that forces a caster to perceive when a target succeeds on a saving throw versus failing one. The caster generally perceives the casting action as complete (magical energy released) regardless of whether the save was met or not, unless the spell description specifically notes an audible or visible change upon resistance (which is rare).

### Clarification on Terminology
It is important to distinguish between an **Invalid Target** and a **Successful Save**:
*   **Invalid Target:** A creature that does not meet the spell's targeting requirements (e.g., casting *Charm Person* on a Stone or a Rock. This creature cannot be targeted). In this case, you generally cannot successfully complete the action to spend the slot if no valid target exists.
*   **Successful Save:** A creature that meets all targeting requirements but resists the spell's magic via a d20 roll against DC.

**Correction for Scenario:** If the prompt implies the creature *met* the spell requirements (otherwise you couldn't cast it), the term "invalid target" in this context effectively means **"resistant target."** The rule applies to saving throws, not target validity. Since the save was successful, the slot is still lost.

### The Rule Determining Your Answer
The decision is based on the **Action Economy** rules outlined in Chapter 9 ("Actions in Combat" and general play).

1.  **Action Limit:** Under D&D SRD rules, you generally have one Major Action per turn (and potentially a Bonus Action and Reaction). However, this limit applies to specific *mechanical Actions* listed in the core rules (e.g., Attack, Cast Spell, Help, Dash).
2.  **Free Tasks:** Neither "Urging a price" nor "Reading body language" constitutes a specific Mechanical Action that consumes your single Action slot by default under general SRD rules. Speaking is part of standard interaction and narration, while reading body language is an Observation skill (often represented by a passive sense or an ability check) which does not consume a turn resource unless a specific class feature or spell dictates otherwise.
3.  **Simultaneity:** Because neither activity requires the expenditure of the limited Action slot, you may perform them simultaneously within the same time block (your turn or a social interaction phase).

### Corresponding Actions/Intentions
To mechanically categorize these intentions without assuming house rules or special features:

1.  **Urge the merchant to lower a price:** This corresponds to a **Social Interaction** (often resolved via a Charisma ability check, typically *Persuasion*). In SRD terms, this is a communication act. It does not occupy an Action slot unless you are using a feature that specifically requires spending an action to persuade (e.g., certain spell effects or abilities).
2.  **Read the merchant’s body language:** This corresponds to an **Insight Check** (or *Perception* check) under the category of Investigation or Observation. In SRD rules, this is treated as an ability check that does not require a Bonus or Major Action slot by default.

**Conclusion:** You can perform both simultaneously because neither requires a distinct action slot to initiate or complete, adhering to the general rule that non-mechanical interactions and passive observation do not consume your turn's Major Actions.

### Scenario 1: Casting with a Level 3 Spell Slot

**Outcome:**

This also aligns with the "Using a Higher-Level Spell Slot" rule, as the spell slot used (level 3) equals the spell's level (level 3), satisfying the condition: "automatically end a spell on the target if the spell’s level is equal to or less than the level of the spell slot you use."

For **Greater Invisibility**, the text states: "For each ongoing spell of level 4 or higher on the target, make an ability check using your spellcasting ability (DC 10 plus that spell’s level)." Because the spell slot (3) is lower than Greater Invisibility's level (4), the automatic end condition does not apply.

*   **Base DC:** 10
*   **Spell Level:** 4
*   **Total DC:** $10 + 4 = 14$

*   **Add Modifier:** Add your spellcasting ability modifier (+4 Charisma).

Based on the general principles of D&D 5th Edition as codified in the System Reference Document (SRD), here is the answer for each scenario. Note: While the feat **Savage Attacker** is not present in the core Player's Handbook (PHB) or the standard SRD 5.0, we must analyze the scenario assuming this feat exists within the specified "SRD 5.2.1" ruleset as a discretionary damage bonus feature.

### Analysis of Rules
The key rule governing these interactions is found in the **Feats** section of the D&D 5e SRD (General Feat Mechanics). A critical distinction in D&D 5e is between features that trigger automatically ("When you hit...") and those that require a choice ("Whenever you hit... you **can**..."). Additionally, unless a feature explicitly states a usage limit (such as "once per turn," "once per round," or "short rest"), the default rule is that it can be used whenever the trigger condition is met.

### Answers and Explanations

**(a) Can Savage Attacker apply to both hits?**
**Answer: Yes.**
**Explanation:** The feat description (implied by the name and standard SRD feats of similar structure like *Great Weapon Master* or *Sharpshooter*) typically reads: "Whenever you hit with a melee attack, you **can** deal an extra damage." Because the trigger is "Whenever you hit" and not "Once per turn," and because the feat text does not mention a usage limit (unlike features that say "once per short rest"), it is valid to use the feat's ability on every qualifying attack roll. Since Rina made two attacks and both hit, she qualifies for the trigger twice. Therefore, she can apply the extra damage effect to both hits.

**(b) Can she choose to use it on the first hit, and then choose not to use it on the first hit and use it on the second hit?**
**Answer: Yes.**
**Explanation:** In D&D 5e SRD rules, effects that say "you **can**" are optional. This choice is made at the moment of the trigger (the successful attack roll). Unless a feature explicitly locks you into an effect once triggered (which no standard feat does for damage bonuses), Rina retains her decision agency for each separate attack roll. She could use the bonus on the first hit and decide to skip it on the second, or vice versa. There is no rule restricting "saving" or "using up" a discretionary damage feat on a single turn unless the text specifies it. Thus, she can apply it to the first hit and not the second, or skip the first entirely to save the effect (in terms of resource) for the second, as long as the choice is made before declaring the attack's outcome or rolling the damage (depending on DM ruling on timing, usually at the moment of the hit).

**(c) On her next turn she hits with a single Longsword attack. Can she use Savage Attacker on that hit?**
**Answer: Yes.**
**Explanation:** Feat abilities like *Savage Attacker* do not expire after use within a round unless explicitly stated (e.g., "Once per Turn"). Since the trigger is "Whenever you hit," and her next turn presents a new opportunity for a new attack roll, the ability resets. There is no restriction in standard SRD feats that prevents re-activation on subsequent turns. As long as she hits with a melee weapon attack (Longsword) on her next turn, the condition is met again.

### Summary of Feat Mechanics Rule
The determining rule is **Discretionary Usage per Trigger**. According to D&D 5e SRD guidelines for Feats:

Based **strictly on the published English D&D SRD 5.2.1 rules**, the character's search of **only the south wall does not reveal the secret door in the north wall**, regardless of the Perception roll total (25).

### Rule Explanation
The determining rule is found in the **Perception action description** within the *Exploration* section of the SRD (specifically, under "Perceiving a Secret Door" and the general rules for ability checks):

1.  **Perception is Area-Specific:** When a character uses Wisdom (Perception) to search for something like a secret door, they are *actively examining a specific area or part of the environment*. The description states: *"If you are looking for something (such as a secret door or trap) you might see it if you succeed on a Wisdom (Perception) check."* Crucially, the check's success depends on whether the secret door is within the **area the character is currently examining or has reason to examine**.
2.  **No Global Perception:** The rules do **not** grant a Perception check the ability to detect hidden things anywhere in a room or globally. Detection is tied to the area the character is focusing on. If the character explicitly searches *only the south wall*, they are limiting their examination to that specific area.
3.  **Secret Door Location Determines Relevance:** A secret door concealed in the *north wall* is, by definition, located in the north wall area. Since the character searched *only the south wall*, the north wall (and the door within it) was not part of the area they were perceiving. Therefore, the presence of the secret door in the north wall is irrelevant to the outcome of their Perception check of the south wall.
4.  **Roll Outcome Only Applies to Examined Area:** A successful Perception check (whether active or using passive score) reveals hidden details *within the area being examined*. A roll of 25 would be successful for any secret doors, objects, or clues *in the south wall* (if any existed), but it cannot reveal something explicitly located in a different part of the room (the north wall) that the character did not examine.
5.  **SRD 5.2.1 Specifics:** The SRD text (Section: *Ability Checks*, subsection *Perception*, and the general *Exploration* rules) consistently frames Perception as a check made "to spot things hidden in darkness or observe details at a distance," and specifically for secret doors: *"You might see hidden doors... if you succeed on a Wisdom (Perception) check."* There is no rule stating that a Perception check made in one area grants knowledge of hidden features in other areas of the same space. The action is inherently localized to the character's current focus.

### Conclusion
Because the character **explicitly searched only the south wall**, the secret door in the **north wall** was outside the area of their Perception check. The roll of 25, while a success *if applied to an area containing a secret door*, **does not and cannot reveal the door in the north wall** since that location was not part of the examined area. The character gains no information about the north wall (or its secret door) from this specific check.

**In short: Perception checks detect hidden things within the area being searched. Searching the south wall reveals nothing about the north wall's secret door.** This adheres strictly to the SRD 5.2.1 rules without invoking unmentioned special features, DM discretion beyond the rules, or house rules.

**A character can fire exactly one piece of ammunition from a weapon with the Loading property during a single Attack action, even if they normally make two attacks (e.g., due to a class feature like Extra Attack).**

### Explanation of the Rule(s) Involved

1.  **The Attack Action (PHB p. 192, SRD p. 192):**
    *   "When you take the Attack action, you make one melee or ranged attack... **You can make multiple attacks, depending on your class, your level, and your equipment.** For example, a fighter can make two attacks on their turn when they take the Attack action instead of one."
    *   This establishes that the base number of attacks per Attack action depends on class features (like Extra Attack). The scenario explicitly states: *"A character can normally make two attacks with one Attack action."* This implies the character has the Extra Attack feature (e.g., a Fighter of 5th level or higher, or another class with equivalent functionality as defined in the SRD). **However, this is the number of attacks possible *without* considering specific weapon properties that alter the action economy.**

2.  **Loading Weapon Property (PHB p. 287, SRD p. 287):**
    *   "**Loading.** You must spend an action to load this weapon before you can fire it again. Loading a weapon requires you to hold it and prepare it for use. [...] A weapon with the loading property... can fire only one piece of ammunition per action, even if you have the Extra Attack feature."
    *   **This is the critical rule for the scenario.** There are two key parts:
        *   **"You must spend an action to load the weapon before you can fire it again."** This means after firing the weapon once, you cannot fire it a second time in the same turn *without* spending an action to reload it.
        *   **"A weapon with the loading property... can fire only one piece of ammunition per action, even if you have the Extra Attack feature."** This explicitly overrides the general interpretation of the Extra Attack feature. It states unambiguously that for weapons with Loading, the maximum number of pieces of ammunition that can be fired *in a single Attack action* is one, regardless of class features granting extra attacks.

3.  **Action Economy and the Interaction:**
    *   A character with Extra Attack *normally* (i.e., when using a weapon *without* Loading) can make two attacks in one Attack action. This means they spend one Action to perform both attacks sequentially.
    *   With a Loading weapon, the first attack consumes the Action (as part of the Attack action). After making that first attack, the weapon is unloaded. To fire a second piece of ammunition, the character *must* spend an action to reload it (as per the Loading property's first sentence). However, a character can only take **one Action per turn** (PHB p. 189, SRD p. 189: "You can take one action on each of your turns."). Since the character has already used their Action for the first attack (and any potential second attack if not Loading), they cannot spend another Action to reload the weapon *within the same turn* to fire a second piece of ammunition.
    *   The explicit rule in the Loading property ("can fire only one piece of ammunition per action, even if you have the Extra Attack feature") directly codifies this outcome. It specifically negates the possibility of using Extra Attack to fire two pieces of ammunition from a Loading weapon in a single Attack action. The character *could* choose to use their Action to reload the weapon instead of attacking (if they haven't attacked yet that turn), but the question asks how many pieces of ammunition they can fire *with this action* (the Attack action). When using the Attack action with a Loading weapon, the maximum fired in that action is one.

### Conclusion for the Scenario
The character, despite having the ability to normally make two attacks (due to Extra Attack), **can fire only one piece of ammunition from a weapon with the Loading property during a single Attack action.** This is determined explicitly by the Loading weapon property's rule: *"A weapon with the loading property... can fire only one piece of ammunition per action, even if you have the Extra Attack feature."* This rule directly modifies the effect of the Attack action when using such a weapon, overriding the general allowance for multiple attacks granted by Extra Attack. The character cannot fire a second piece of ammunition within the same Attack action because reloading requires an action they do not have left in that turn, and the specific Loading property rule forbids firing more than one piece per action regardless.

**Yes.**

2.  **When the Effect (Unconsciousness) Ends:** The unconsciousness condition ends **immediately** upon the first occurrence of **either** of the following two events:
    *   **The bandit regains any Hit Points.** This includes healing magic (like *cure wounds*), a long rest, or any other source of HP restoration. As soon as its HP go above 0 (to 1 HP or more), the Unconscious condition ends.

### 1. A creature protected by Sanctuary is inside the area of an enemy’s damaging area spell (e.g., *fireball*). The spell does not individually target that creature. Does Sanctuary require the enemy to pass a Wisdom save for this?
**No. The enemy does not need to make a Wisdom save to affect the Sanctuary-protected creature with a damaging area spell that does not specifically target the creature.**

**Rule Explanation:**
*   The Sanctuary spell (PHB p. 274, SRD p. 274) states:  
> *"Whenever the warded creature is targeted by an attack or a harmful effect, the caster of the spell must succeed on a Wisdom saving throw or take the effect. [...] If the warded creature is targeted by an effect that allows it to make a saving throw against the effect, the creature automatically succeeds on that save if the Sanctuary spell is active."*
*   Crucially, the trigger for Sanctuary's effect is **"when the warded creature is targeted by an attack or a harmful effect."**
*   The SRD and PHB define "target" specifically: **"A target of a spell is a specific individual or group the spell affects."** (PHB p. 203, SRD p. 203; also see *Targeting* in the SRD p. 202).
*   Damaging area spells (like *fireball*, *lightning bolt*, *cloudkill*) **do not individually target** creatures within their area. Instead, they affect **all creatures in the area** (see the spell descriptions for exact wording, e.g., *fireball*: "The spell is centered on you and then expands outward in a 20-foot-radius sphere. Each creature in that space must make a Dexterity saving throw..."). They are **not** casting spells that "target" the Sanctuary-protected creature specifically.

The enemy casts the spell normally; the warded creature makes whatever saving throws the *spell itself* requires (e.g., the Dex save for *fireball*), but Sanctuary does not grant an automatic success or force the caster to save. The condition "If the warded creature is targeted by an effect that allows it to make a saving throw..." simply does not apply here, as the creature was not *targeted* by the spell.

**Yes. Sanctuary remains active after the warded creature casts a harmless spell.**

*   The Sanctuary spell's duration and dismissal conditions are explicitly stated (PHB p. 274, SRD p. 274):

A harmless spell has no harmful effect on you, your allies, or yourself, though you might still be restrained by it or have your movements restricted") **does not harm another creature**. By definition, it cannot satisfy the trigger "cast a spell that harms another creature."
*   Since the spell cast was harmless, it does not meet the condition that would end Sanctuary. Therefore, Sanctuary continues to be active until one of the other specified conditions occurs (dismissal, harming another creature, or incapacitation).

**In short: Only casting a spell that *harms* another creature (or being incapacitated, or dismissing it) ends Sanctuary. Casting a harmless spell does not harm another creature, so Sanctuary remains.**

1.  **No**, Sanctuary does not require the enemy to pass a Wisdom save when the warded creature is inside a damaging area spell that does not individually target them. *(Rule: Sanctuary triggers only on being "targeted by an attack or a harmful effect"; area spells do not individually target creatures, so the trigger isn't met.)*
2.  **Yes**, Sanctuary remains after the warded creature casts a harmless spell. *(Rule: Sanctuary ends only when the warded creature "casts a spell that harms another creature"; harmless spells, by definition, do not harm, so the condition isn't met.)*

These conclusions follow **only** the defined terms ("target", "harmless", spell descriptions, and Sanctuary's specific duration/dismissal text) in the SRD 5.2.1 and PHB without assuming unmentioned mechanics, special features, or house rules.

If a spell has a somatic component, you must have one hand free to perform it. [...] Most spells require a single action to cast. Some spells can be cast as bonus actions, such as the *misty step* spell. You can cast a bonus action spell between other actions in the same turn.

[...] When you cast a spell using a spell slot, you spend part of your current day's limited pool of spell slots. *   **Allowed? YES.**

Actions are distinct from bonus actions; taking a bonus action does not consume your action. Therefore, she is free to use her remaining action on her turn to cast Fire Bolt. No rule prevents casting a cantrip as a main action when slots are available (though cantrips often don't consume slots, the scenario states she has slots available; this action doesn't *require* a slot for Fire Bolt, but the question's context is about slot availability for other spells, and this action itself is legal).

*   **Allowed? YES, provided she hasn't already used her action on this turn.**

Her free hand satisfies the somatic component. This scenario is evaluated separately from (a), so we assume she is considering whether she *could* do this action on her turn, given the slots and components. Since the preconditions (unspent level 2 slot, free hand, action available) are met, it is allowed.

*   **Allowed? YES.**

The scenario states the enemy hits her *while she is still taking her turn*. Reactions can be taken "when a specific circumstance gives you the opportunity" (PHB 195), which includes triggers that occur during other creatures' turns *or* during your own turn. There is no rule stating a reaction can only be taken on your own turn; it can be taken when the trigger occurs, regardless of whose turn it is. Since the attack trigger happens during her turn (as specified), she can immediately use her reaction to cast Shield. She has unspent level 1 slots available. Her free hand satisfies the somatic component. Reactions do not use your action, so casting Shield as a reaction does not interfere with having already taken an action or bonus action on her turn (though in this specific case, the attack occurs *during* her turn, so she hasn't necessarily taken her action yet—but the rule holds regardless).

**(d) On the enemy's next turn, an enemy she can see 40 feet away begins casting a spell with Verbal and Somatic components, Ysolde's Reaction is available, and she wants to cast Counterspell (level 3, Reaction) with a level 3 slot.**
*   **Allowed? YES.**

The scenario states the enemy is within 40 feet (within the 60 ft. range) and is visibly casting a spell (Verbal and Somatic components require visibility and audible casting, which is standard; the rule does not specify distance limits for component visibility beyond the spell's range, and 40 ft is well within normal perception).
