Under the SRD 5.2.1 *Sanctuary* spell

> *The spell places a ward on a creature... The ward lasts for the duration, or until dispelled or broken. The ward prevents the warded creature from being targeted by spells or attacks. In addition, any creature that targets the warded creature with an attack or a harmful spell must make a Wisdom saving throw… If the warded creature makes an attack or casts a spell that affects an enemy creature, the spell ends.*

The ward is triggered only by **targeting** the warded creature.

* Attack or harmful spell **targeting** the warded creature → the attacker / caster must make a Wisdom save vs the Sanctuary save DC or lose the action. The spell does not say “affects” in this clause, it says “targets… with an attack or a harmful spell”.

An area-of-effect damaging spell that does not *individually* target the warded creature does not “target” that creature. The creature is simply in the area. The spell’s description is “each creature in the area”, not “target one creature”. Sanctuary’s saving-throw clause is therefore not invoked by an enemy dropping a fireball, cone of cold, etc. over the warded creature, because the enemy is not targeting the warded creature. The warded creature still takes the normal area damage; Sanctuary does not stop area effects that don’t specifically target it.

The ward is broken by the warded creature’s own actions:

> *If the warded creature makes an attack or casts a spell that affects an enemy creature, the spell ends.*

It is the warded creature’s casting, not the enemy’s, that can end the ward, and only if the spell *affects an enemy creature*. 

Casting a harmless spell — e.g. *mage hand* at an object, *detect magic*, *light* on self, *cure wounds* on an ally, or any spell that does not affect an enemy creature — does not meet the “casts a spell that affects an enemy creature” condition. The ward therefore remains in effect.

If the harmless spell were one that does affect an enemy, even indirectly, the ward would end. The mere act of casting a spell is not enough; the spell must affect an enemy creature.

Under SRD 5.2.1 a character can only cast one leveled spell per round in a very specific way.

* PHB / SRD Spellcasting rules: A spell’s casting time tells you how long it takes to cast the spell. *Bonus Action* is a casting time. 

* If you cast a spell with a bonus action casting time, the bonus-action spell rule applies:

> *A spell cast with a bonus action is especially swift... You can’t cast another spell during the same turn, except for a cantrip with a casting time of 1 action.*

The restriction is tied to the turn on which the bonus-action spell is cast, not to the action economy per se. It forbids casting any other spell of 1st level or higher on that same turn. A cantrip with a casting time of 1 action is the only exception.

Misty Step is a 2nd-level spell with a casting time of Bonus Action. Ysolde has just cast it on her turn, using a 2nd level slot. The restriction is now in effect for the remainder of that turn.

a) *Cast the Fire Bolt cantrip with her Magic action.* 
Allowed. Fire Bolt is a cantrip with a casting time of 1 action. That is the specific exception to the bonus-action spell rule. She has a free hand for Somatic components and the cantrip does not require a spell slot. She can use her Action to cast it.

b) *Cast Scorching Ray, level 2, Magic action, with another spell slot.* 
Not allowed on that turn. Scorching Ray is a 2nd level spell with a casting time of 1 action. Casting it would be a second leveled spell on the same turn on which a bonus-action spell was cast. The bonus-action spell rule forbids any other spell except a cantrip with a casting time of 1 action. She has unspent 2nd and 3rd level slots, but she may not use them for Scorching Ray this turn.

c) *Cast Shield as a Reaction while she is still taking her turn.*
Not allowed on that turn. The reaction would be used during the same turn on which Misty Step was cast. The bonus-action spell rule limits all spells you cast on that turn, not just spells cast with your Action. Shield is a 1st level spell with a casting time of Reaction. It is not a cantrip with a casting time of 1 action, so casting it on the same turn as the bonus-action Misty Step violates the rule, even though the casting time is Reaction. The restriction is “during the same turn”, and the attack trigger occurs while Ysolde’s turn is still ongoing.

If the trigger for the reaction occurred on a different turn, Shield would be permissible, subject to the normal reaction rules and the 1st level slot.

d) *On the enemy’s next turn, cast Counterspell as a Reaction with a 3rd level slot.*
Allowed. The bonus-action spell restriction applies only to the turn on which the bonus-action spell was cast. The enemy’s next turn is a new turn. Ysolde’s Reaction is available, she can see the enemy 40 ft away, the enemy is beginning to cast a spell with Verbal and Somatic components, and Counterspell has a casting time of Reaction. She has an unspent 3rd level slot, so she may cast Counterspell.

In short: a is permitted by the cantrip exception, b and c are prohibited by the bonus-action spell restriction for the turn Misty Step was cast, and d is on a later turn and is therefore unrestricted.

In SRD 5.2.1 *Animate Trees* is not a power that the animated object itself gains.

*Animate Trees* is a transmutation spell

* **Range:** 100 feet
* **Target:** up to five trees you can see within range that are within 100 feet of each other
* **Effect:** you imbue each tree with a semblance of life. An animated tree is an object that is under your control. It is not a creature and it does not gain the spellcasting ability of the caster. It has the statistics of an animated tree: AC 13, 74 hp, speed 0, slam 2d6+4 bludgeoning, and it is friendly to you and your companions.

The spell gives the tree no action economy of its own apart from the slam it can make when you command it, and it certainly does not give it the innate spellcasting trait that a treant has. An animated tree is an object animated by magic, not a treant and not a creature with innate spellcasting. It cannot cast *Animate Trees* or any other spell. The attempt to “use Animate Trees itself” therefore does nothing; the tree has no ability to cast spells.

Control and distance

The spell’s control is tied to the caster, the treant in this case. The SRD text for the spell is:

*The trees remain animated for 1 day or until you dismiss the spell as an action. The trees are friendly to you and your companions. If you are more than 100 feet away from an animated tree, you lose control of it and it reverts to normal.*

While the tree is within 100 feet of the treant that animated it, and less than one day has passed and the spell has not been dismissed, it stays animated and remains under the treant’s control.

Once the animated tree is moved to 125 feet from the original treant, the distance condition is violated:

* The tree is still animated for the remainder of the 1-day duration, because the duration is not ended by movement.
* The treant no longer has control of it because the tree is more than 100 feet away. The tree is no longer friendly to the treant and its companions and it will act independently, which for an animated tree means it ceases to take commanded actions and effectively reverts to a normal, inert tree.

If the tree were to be brought back within 100 feet of the treant before the 1-day duration expires, control would be regained. After 1 day, or if the treant uses *Animate Trees* again, the trees revert to normal regardless of distance.

In SRD 5.2.1 an Opportunity Attack is a special reaction. 

* Opportunity Attacks
* *You can make an opportunity attack when a hostile creature that you can see moves out of your reach.*
* *You can make only one opportunity attack per round, and you can take the attack only when the creature that provokes it moves out of your reach.*

The triggering condition is a hostile creature **moving out of your reach**. The movement has to be movement of the creature itself and it has to be the creature’s own movement, i.e. willing movement.

* PHB / SRD: The attack is made as a reaction when a hostile creature leaves your reach. It is not made when you are forced to move the creature.
* Teleportation is not movement for the purpose of opportunity attacks. Misty Step is a teleportation effect: *You teleport...* A creature that teleports does not move through the intervening space and does not leave reach by moving; it disappears from reach. Teleportation therefore does not provoke an opportunity attack.
* Forced movement does not provoke. A push, pull or slide imposed by a spell such as Thunderwave moves the target, but the target is not voluntarily moving and is not “moving out of your reach” on its own. The cleric is hurled 10 ft away without using any of the cleric’s movement or actions, so no opportunity attack is provoked by the cleric.

The fighter’s move is the only one that satisfies the trigger.

* The fighter is hostile to the ogre, the ogre can see her and the fighter uses her own Speed to walk 20 ft away.
* Leaving the ogre’s 5-ft reach on a voluntary move is the classic opportunity attack trigger. The first 5 ft of that walk moves the fighter out of the ogre’s reach.

The ogre’s reaction is therefore available for that creature and only for that creature.

An opportunity attack is a single attack, not the creature’s normal Multiattack:

*You make a single melee attack against the provoking creature.* 

An ogre’s melee attack is its normal melee weapon attack. By the stat block the ogre makes a melee weapon attack with its greatclub, +6 to hit, reach 5 ft, one target, 2d8+4 bludgeoning damage. That is the attack the ogre can make as a reaction against the fighter. The wizard’s Misty Step and the cleric’s Thunderwave push do not provoke.

Under the SRD the Loading property limits ammunition expenditure per use of the weapon, not per Attack action.

* Loading
  *You can fire only one piece of ammunition from a Loading weapon when you use an action, a Bonus Action, or a Reaction to fire it, regardless of the number of attacks you can normally make.*

An Attack action that would normally give two attacks — e.g. Extra Attack — is still *one use of an action to fire it*. The Loading property says you can fire only one piece of ammunition when you use an action to fire it, regardless of the number of attacks you can normally make.

Therefore the character can fire only 1 piece of ammunition from the Loading weapon with that Attack action. The second attack granted by Extra Attack cannot be made with the Loading weapon because a second piece of ammunition would be fired with the same action, which Loading forbids. The limit is one ammunition per action/bonus action/reaction, not one ammunition per attack.

answers.candidate_answer:
In the SRD 5.2.1 the feat list is closed and a character may only take a feat that is actually published in the SRD, and only if it meets its prerequisites.

* **Grappler**
The SRD 5.2.1 feat *Grappler* has no prerequisites.

> **Grappler**
> *You are particularly adept at grappling and pinning your foes.*
> ...
The feat is therefore available to any character who can take a feat, regardless of class, ability scores or fighting style. Selu is a Fighter 1 / Wizard 4 and is gaining a feat on reaching Wizard 4. Strength 10 and Dexterity 14 do not prevent the choice. The existing Defense fighting style does not interact with Grappler. Selu can take Grappler.

* **Archery**
*Archery* is not a feat in the SRD 5.2.1. It is a Fighting Style option:

> **Fighting Styles**
> *Archery.* You gain a +2 bonus to attack rolls you make with ranged weapons.

Fighting styles are class features gained by fighters, rangers, paladins, etc., not feats. The SRD 5.2.1 does not contain a feat named *Archery* and does not contain a general feat *Fighting Style* or *Fighting Initiate* that would let a character pick up a fighting style as a feat. Selu already has the Defense fighting style from Fighter 1. With the SRD material alone there is no mechanism for Selu to gain the Archery fighting style, let alone take “Archery” as a feat.

* **Boon of Combat Prowess**
*Boon of Combat Prowess* is not a feat in the SRD 5.2.1. The SRD feat list is: Actor, Athlete, Charger, Crossbow Expert, Defensive Duelist, Dual Wielder, Dungeon Delver, Healer, Inspiring Leader, Keen Mind, Linguist, Magic Initiate, Martial Adept, Medium Armour Master, Mobile, Mounted Combatant, Observant, Polearm Master, Sentinel, Sharpshooter, Shield Master, Skilled, Skulker, Tavern Brawler, Tough, Weapon Master, and the fighting styles are class features. There is no *Boon of Combat Prowess* feat in that list, and no general rule in the SRD that allows a character to take a non-SRD option. Selu cannot take it under published SRD 5.2.1 rules.

So under strict SRD 5.2.1, Grappler is permissible, Archery is not a feat at all, and Boon of Combat Prowess is not a published SRD option.

In D&D 5.2.1 a spell is not “cast” until the casting is completed and the targets are chosen. The spellcasting rules are:

* *Choosing Targets.* You choose the targets of your spell when you cast it, and you must be able to see them. The spell’s description tells you what information you need to pick targets, and the description tells you the spell’s range.
* *Range.* A spell’s range is the distance from you that the spell can reach. A spell’s range must include its target at the instant you finish casting.

If a target you try to pick does not meet the spell’s requirements for target, range, line of effect, etc., you cannot legally choose it. The rules do not allow you to “cast at” an invalid target and then have the spell fizzle after the slot is spent; you must be able to identify a valid target as part of the act of casting.

In practice this is handled at the table as:

* **The spell slot is expended** if you begin casting. Completing a spell’s casting time and components expends the spell slot even if the spell later has no effect, e.g. because all targets succeed on a saving throw. The slot is not refunded because the casting was completed.
* **The target is unaffected.** A spell simply does not apply to a creature that is not a valid target for it. A spell that would normally have no effect on a target that succeeds on its saving throw still has no effect on an invalid target; there is nothing to apply the effect to. Immunity, invalid type, out of range, total cover, etc., all mean the spell’s effect never reaches the creature.
* **What the caster perceives.** The caster knows whether the chosen creature is a valid target for the spell as part of choosing the target. You must be able to see the target and the target must be within range and of a type the spell can target. If the creature is not of a targetable type — e.g. the spell targets “a creature you can see within 30 ft.” and the creature is 60 ft. away, behind total cover, or is an object/unattended item and the spell targets only creatures — the caster recognises that the creature cannot be targeted when the spell is being cast. If a DM allows the casting to be attempted anyway, the spell fails to be completed, the slot is expended and the caster perceives the spell’s magic dissipating with no effect, just as with a successful save where the spell normally has no effect on the target.

That is the same outcome the rules give for a target that is immune or that succeeds on the save the spell calls for: the spell is cast, the slot is gone, and the target is not affected, the caster perceives the spell’s energy going off but having no effect on the invalid/un- affected target.

No. Under the general action rules in SRD 5.2.1 the principle is *One Thing at a Time*.

* You can take only one action at a time. This principle is most important in combat, as explained in “Combat” later in “Playing the Game.”

The SRD gives the social-interaction example that is on point:

* Actions can come up in other situations, too: in a social interaction, you can try to Influence a creature or use the Search action to read the creature’s body language, but you can’t do both at the same time.

The two intentions you describe map to those two actions:

* **Urge a merchant to lower a price** is an attempt to change the merchant’s attitude / get the merchant to do something for you. That is the social *Influence* action. Influence is the action used to persuade, deceive, intimidate, etc., a creature in a social interaction.

* **Reading the merchant’s body language** is the *Search* action used socially to read a creature’s body language / cues.

Because the general rule is one action at a time, the character can do one of those on a given action and not the other at the same time. He could Influence on one action and Search on a later action, but the SRD explicitly says you can’t do both simultaneously in a social interaction. No special feature changes the normal action rules in this scenario, so the One Thing at a Time restriction applies.

Under SRD 5.2.1 *Sanctuary*:

*Sanctuary* 1st-level abjuration
> You ward a creature within range. Until the spell ends, any creature who **targets the warded creature with an attack roll or a damaging spell** must succeed on a Wisdom saving throw or either choose a new target or lose the attack or spell. **This spell doesn’t protect the warded creature from areas of effect.** The spell ends if the warded creature makes an attack roll, casts a spell, or deals damage.

1. **Damaging area spell that does not individually target the warded creature**

Sanctuary only imposes the Wisdom save when a creature *targets the warded creature* with an attack roll or a damaging spell.

An area-of-effect damaging spell does not target the warded creature individually; it targets a point or area. The spell’s text expressly carves that out:

* “This spell doesn’t protect the warded creature from areas of effect.”

Therefore the warded creature is not protected from the area damage at all, and no Wisdom save is triggered by the enemy. The enemy is free to include the warded creature in the area and the warded creature takes the area damage normally.

The “targets the warded creature with... a damaging spell” clause would only apply to a spell that *does* target the warded creature, e.g. *scorching ray* aimed at the warded creature, *magic missile* targeted at the warded creature. An AoE like *fireball*, *shatter*, *burning hands* etc. is not a targeting spell for Sanctuary’s purposes, and in any case the explicit “doesn’t protect... from areas of effect” overrides it.

2. **The warded creature casts a harmless spell**

The duration clause is:

> The spell ends if the warded creature makes an attack roll, casts a spell, or deals damage.

There is no “harmless” exception. Casting a spell is a condition that ends Sanctuary regardless of the spell’s level, school, or whether it deals damage or targets anyone. The warded creature casting *any* spell, even a harmless *mage hand* or *detect magic*, ends *Sanctuary* immediately.

So Sanctuary is lost the moment the warded creature casts a spell.

Under the SRD 5.2.1 social interaction rules an NPC’s attitude does not by itself grant advantage or disadvantage on the Charisma check that is the Influence attempt. Attitude is a fictional positioning factor that the DM uses to set the difficulty of the check and to decide whether the attempt is even possible.

The SRD sets out the Social Interaction activity as:

* The DM determines the creature’s starting attitude toward the character. The three base attitudes are Hostile, Indifferent and Friendly. 
* The DM then sets a Charisma check DC for the attempt to shift the attitude or to get the creature to do something. The DC is set by the DM based on the attitude, the reasonableness of the request and the creature’s personality.

That is, the attitude changes the DC, not the roll mechanics:

* A Friendly creature is inclined to help the character. A reasonable request from a Friendly creature is easier. The DM sets a lower DC for a Persuasion/Deception/Intimidation check to influence a Friendly NPC, and the NPC is more likely to be willing to listen in the first place.
* A Hostile creature is actively opposed to the character. A reasonable request from a Hostile creature is harder, or may be impossible until the attitude is improved. The DM sets a higher DC for a Persuasion/Deception/Intimidation check to influence a Hostile NPC, and the NPC may refuse to even engage in the social interaction.

Hesitant is the DM’s assessment of how the NPC feels about the specific request, not a mechanical condition. A hesitant NPC is still making the check, but the DC reflects that hesitation.

Because you state neither check has any other source of Advantage or Disadvantage, the two Influence checks are both made with a straight d20 + Charisma check modifier. The only difference between the two NPCs is the DC the DM assigns for each one based on Friendly vs Hostile attitude, with the Hostile NPC having a higher DC and the Friendly NPC having a lower DC for the same request. No automatic advantage is gained from being Friendly and no automatic disadvantage is imposed for being Hostile under the base SRD social rules.

Rage is not instantaneous, it has a duration that is renewed.

*Duration.* The Rage lasts until the end of your next turn, and it ends early if you don Heavy armor or have the Incapacitated condition.

Rage is started in round 1 as a Bonus Action. 
Rage started on Dara’s turn in round 1 therefore lasts until the end of Dara’s next turn, i.e. the end of round 2.

> If your Rage is still active on your next turn, you can extend the Rage for another round by doing one of the following:
> • Make an attack roll against an enemy.
> • Force an enemy to make a saving throw.
> • Take a Bonus Action to extend your Rage.
> Each time the Rage is extended, it lasts until the end of your next turn.

The check to extend is made on the start of the turn on which the Rage would otherwise expire. At the start of Dara’s turn in round 2 the Rage is still active because it was started in round 1 and lasts until the end of round 2. On that turn Dara must do one of the three extension triggers, otherwise the Rage will expire at the end of round 2.

### Scenario A
Dara takes the Attack action and misses with both attacks against an enemy.

An attack roll is an attack roll whether it hits or misses. The extension condition is *Make an attack roll against an enemy*, not *hit* with an attack roll. Dara has made an attack roll against an enemy on her turn in round 2, so the Rage is extended.

Each time the Rage is extended, it lasts until the end of your next turn. The extension therefore lasts until the end of Dara’s next turn, i.e. the end of round 3.

The Rage is still active when Dara’s turn begins in round 3. It will expire at the end of round 3 unless it is extended again on the round 3 turn.

### Scenario B
Dara only moves and takes the Dodge action, with no attack roll and no saving throw.

On Dara’s turn in round 2 she does not make an attack roll against an enemy, she does not force an enemy to make a saving throw, and she does not take the Bonus Action to extend her Rage. Dodge uses no Bonus Action and the movement does not satisfy any of the three extension conditions.

The Rage therefore is not extended. It expires at the end of the turn on which it was started to last to, the end of round 2, per *The Rage lasts until the end of your next turn*.

The Rage is not active when Dara’s turn begins in round 3.

To keep the Rage going without attacking in that scenario Dara could have used the permitted non-attack extension:

* Take a Bonus Action to extend your Rage.

That is the Bonus Action specifically listed for extension. It does not require an attack roll or forcing a save, and it can be used even while taking the Dodge action, because Dodge is an action. The other non-attack option is to *Force an enemy to make a saving throw* on the turn.

If Dara had used her Bonus Action on the round 2 turn to extend the Rage, the Rage would have been extended to last until the end of round 3, just as in Scenario A, and would still be active at the start of round 3.

Under SRD 5.2.1 the Animate Trees action is defined for a treant as:

* *Animate Trees (1/Day). The treant magically animates up to two trees it can see within 60 feet of itself. Each tree uses the Treant stat block, except it has Intelligence and Charisma scores of 1, it can’t speak, and it lacks this action.*

The “except” clause modifies the stat block that is used for every tree created by the action. The animated tree is a Treant stat block with three specific removals/changes:

* Int 1, Cha 1
* can’t speak
* **lacks this action** – i.e. lacks Animate Trees

An effect only gives what it says it gives. The base Treant stat block includes Animate Trees, but the created tree is explicitly built from that block *except* it lacks this action. Therefore the animated tree does not have the Animate Trees action at all, and cannot use it, even though it otherwise uses the Treant stat block and takes its turn immediately after the treant on the same Initiative count and obeys the treant.

Distance termination is independent of ability to use the action.

* A tree remains animate for 1 day or until it dies, the treant dies, or it is more than 120 feet from the treant. The tree then takes root if possible.

That is a duration condition for the animation effect created by the original treant’s Animate Trees. If the animated tree is alive, the original treant is alive, less than 1 day has passed, and the animated tree becomes more than 120 feet from the original treant, the animation ends. The creature ceases to be an animated Treant and “takes root if possible.”

So in your scenario the animated tree cannot animate further trees because it lacks the Animate Trees action by the explicit exception. If it is moved to 125 ft from the original treant while both are alive and <1 day has passed, the animation terminates by the >120 ft clause and the tree takes root if possible.

Under SRD 5.2.1 a creature at 0 hit points is unconscious and dying unless it is stable.

* Stable
A stable creature at 0 hit points does not make death saving throws. It remains at 0 hit points and will regain hit points on its own. Taking damage ends the stable condition.

* Damage at 0 hit points
> If you take damage while you have 0 hit points, you suffer a death saving throw failure.
> If you take damage that equals or exceeds your hit point maximum, you suffer instant death.

A creature that suffers three death saving throw failures dies. A creature that suffers three successes regains 1 hit point.

The character was dropped to 0 and accumulated 2 death saving throw failures. The ally’s successful DC 10 Wisdom Medicine check stabilized her. While stabilized she does not make death saves and her existing tally of 2 failures / 0 successes is retained.

The trap dart hits her while she is still at 0 hit points and stable.

* The 3 damage is less than her hit point maximum of 24, so it is not instant death by the maximum-HP rule.
* The damage is taken while she has 0 hit points, so she suffers a death saving throw failure by the “damage at 0 hit points” rule.
* Taking damage also removes the stable condition, so she is once again dying and will have to make death saving throws again.

Failures: 2 pre-existing + 1 for the damage = 3 failures. Successes: 0.

Three failures is death. She is dead immediately after the dart hits, she is no longer stable and is not making death saves any more.

Therefore there is no “start of her next turn if she still has 0 hit points” – she is dead at the moment the damage is applied. If the third failure were not applied the character would be unconscious, dying, no longer stable, with 2 failures and 0 successes retained, and at the start of her next turn she would make a death saving throw as normal, with one more failure resulting in death and three successes ending the dying condition.

On a turn you may expend spell slots only once.

*One Spell with a Spell Slot per Turn*
> On a turn, you can expend only one spell slot to cast a spell. This rule means you can’t, for example, cast a spell with a spell slot using the Magic action and another one using a Bonus Action on the same turn.

Ysolde’s turn has already had a spell-slot expenditure.

* Misty Step is a Bonus Action spell and it was cast with a level 2 spell slot. That is the one spell-slot expenditure for that turn.

a) Cast the Fire Bolt cantrip with her Magic action.
Allowed. Cantrips are cast without a spell slot.

> Cantrips. A cantrip is cast without a spell slot.

The “one spell slot per turn” restriction is about expending a slot. A cantrip does not expend a slot, so it can be used on the same turn in which a spell-slot spell was cast with the Bonus Action. Ysolde can therefore take the Magic action to cast Fire Bolt.

b) Cast Scorching Ray (level 2, Magic action) with another spell slot.
Not allowed. Scorching Ray would be a second spell-slot expenditure on the same turn. The rule expressly forbids casting a spell with a spell slot using the Magic action after you have already expended a spell slot with the Bonus Action on the same turn. Ysolde has already expended a level 2 slot for Misty Step this turn.

c) Cast Shield (level 1, Reaction) using a level 1 slot while she is still on her turn.
Not allowed on this turn. A Reaction spell is still cast on your turn if the trigger occurs on your turn.

> A spell that has a casting time of a Reaction is cast in response to a trigger that is defined in the spell’s Casting Time entry.

The trigger “when she would be hit” is occurring during Ysolde’s own turn, so the casting would be on the same turn in which she already expended a spell slot for Misty Step. One spell slot per turn is already exhausted for the turn, and she would be expending a second slot. The per-turn slot limit therefore blocks Shield in that circumstance; a Reaction used on her own turn still counts against the turn’s one-slot limit. In SRD 5.2.1 *Knock* is

* 2nd-level transmutation, range 30 ft., verbal, visible target
* “Choose an object that you can see within range that is held shut by a mundane lock, arcane lock, or a combination of both. The object can be a door, window, box, or chest. *Knock* opens stuck, barred, or locked doors, windows, boxes, or chests, and unlocks a single lock.”

The spell’s effect is on one *object*. If the object is held shut by a lock, the lock is opened. If the object is held shut by more than one lock the spell only affects one of them.

* *Audible component.* “The spell produces a loud knocking noise, audible out to 300 feet.” The loud knock is produced at the point of casting no matter what the result is. It is not a function of whether the object is successfully opened.

Application

**Chest with two mundane locks.**
The chest is one object held shut by two separate mundane locks. *Knock* on the chest can only unlock a single lock. One of the two mundane locks is unlocked by the casting, the second mundane lock remains locked and continues to hold the chest shut. The chest therefore remains closed/held shut.

The casting still produces the spell’s normal audible effect: a loud knocking noise audible out to 300 ft at the point of casting.

**Door held shut only by *Arcane Lock*.**
*Arcane Lock* is a single magical lock. The SRD *Arcane Lock* specifically says the object can be unlocked with *Knock* or by dispelling the *Arcane Lock*. The door is one object held shut by a single lock, even though that lock is magical. *Knock* therefore unlocks that Arcane Lock and the door is opened, assuming it is otherwise not barred or otherwise prevented from opening.

The casting also produces the spell’s normal audible effect: a loud knocking noise audible out to 300 ft at the point of casting.

Under the SRD 5.2.1 action economy the two things you describe are not combat actions at all, and outside of combat there is no action budget that would prevent them from being done together.

* Persuasion and Insight are skills, not actions.

The general rules for ability checks are in SRD 5.2.1: “The DM calls for an ability check when a character or monster attempts an action...” The DM may call for a Persuasion check to see if the character is convincing the merchant to lower a price, and an Insight check to read the merchant’s body language and determine what the merchant really wants or is hiding. Both are skill checks.

Skill checks do not consume Action, Bonus Action, Reaction or Movement, and they are not subject to the combat action rules. The combat action rules in SRD 5.2.1, Chapter 9, only apply in combat. Social / exploration interaction is covered by the general rules for ability checks and the social interaction rules.

Outside of combat the rules do not limit you to one thing at a time. A character can talk and observe at the same time; speaking is part of normal interaction and reading body language is a passive observation that the DM can resolve with an Insight check made at the same time as the Persuasion attempt. In practice the DM will normally resolve the negotiation with a single Persuasion check, and may allow or require an Insight check to gain advantage on that check, or to learn the DC / the merchant’s hidden motive, but both checks can be made in the same exchange.

There is no “simultaneous action” rule because there is no action to take. If you were to force the two intentions into combat terms, neither corresponds to the Attack action, the Use an Object action, the Ready action, etc. Talking to an NPC and observing him are free activities in exploration/social play; they only become an action in combat if the DM rules you are using the Help action, the Use an Object action, etc., which you are not.

If the negotiation were happening in combat, Persuasion would still not be a combat action and could only be attempted if the DM allows it as part of a free interaction, and Insight would be a check the DM allows, not an action you expend. No special feature is required to do both, and no feature is needed to do them “simultaneously” because the normal rules do not prohibit it.

Dispel Magic is cast on a creature. The spell has two parts.

*Base effect*

* *Any ongoing spell of level 3 or lower on the target ends.* No check is required.
* *For each ongoing spell of level 4 or higher on the target, make an ability check using your spellcasting ability (DC 10 plus that spell’s level).* On a successful check the spell ends.

With a level 3 slot the higher-level slot rule does not change the base effect, because the slot is not higher than the spells.

* Haste – level 3. 3 ≤ 3, so it is “level 3 or lower”. It ends automatically.
* Greater Invisibility – level 4. 4 ≥ 4, so it is an ongoing spell of level 4 or higher.

An ability check is required for Greater Invisibility:

DC = 10 + spell level = 10 + 4 = 14

Ability check = d20 + spellcasting ability modifier. The Sorcerer’s spellcasting ability is Charisma, modifier +4.

Check total = d20 + 4. The check succeeds on 14 or more, i.e. d20 ≥ 10.

If the check succeeds Greater Invisibility ends; if it fails it remains. Haste ends in either case.

*Using a Higher-Level Spell Slot*

“You automatically end a spell on the target if the spell’s level is equal to or less than the level of the spell slot you use.”

With a level 4 slot:

* Haste level 3 ≤ 4 → automatically ends.
* Greater Invisibility level 4 ≤ 4 → automatically ends.

The automatic-ending rule replaces the normal level 4+ check. No ability check and no DC 14 is needed; both Haste and Greater Invisibility end.

In 5th edition the Constitution modifier is a part of your hit-point
maximum and not of the Hit Die you roll when you go up a level.

A hit point maximum is built up from

* the hit points you get from the Hit Dice you have rolled when you
went up in level, and
* the Constitution modifier that was in effect when each of those Hit
Dice was rolled.

When the Constitution score itself changes the game does not re-roll
or re-calculate the Hit Dice you have already rolled. It changes the
Constitution component that is added to the maximum you already have.

SRD 5.2.1 Ability Scores

*Whenever your Constitution score changes, your hit point maximum changes by the same amount as your Constitution modifier changes.*

That is the whole mechanical effect of a post-creation change to
Constitution. The increase is a flat change to the current hit point
maximum, not a per-level re-calculation.

Here

* Con 15 → modifier +2
* Con 16 → modifier +3

The Constitution modifier goes up by

+3 − (+2) = +1

so the hit point maximum of the character goes up by the same amount,
+1 hit point, on the character’s current hit point maximum. Current hit
points are raised by the same amount, to a maximum of the new hit point
maximum, and any excess is lost in the usual way.

That is the +1 to the maximum that the rules attach to the +1 to the
Constitution modifier. In play this is often expressed as “+1 hit point
per Hit Die you already possess”, i.e. +1 × the number of Hit Dice the
6th-level character has already rolled, 6 Hit Dice, = +6 hit points of
maximum hit points that are accounted for by the six levels of
Constitution modifier that are now being applied at +3 instead of +2.
The net mechanical effect on the character’s sheet at this moment is
the +1 modifier increase to the maximum, which is the +6 of
Constitution-modifier hit points that the six Hit Dice now carry.

answers.candidate_answer:
Under the 5.2.1 SRD there is no general “non-lethal damage” attack option. A hit that would drop a creature to 0 hit points is resolved by the hit-point / death rules, not by a special capture option.

SRD Combat – Hit Points

> A creature can have a number of hit points that range from 1 to over a hundred or more.
> When damage reduces a creature’s hit points to 0, the creature falls unconscious, its speed becomes 0, and it can’t take actions or reactions.

That is the ordinary result of an attack that reduces a creature to 0 hit points. The SRD also gives the attacker the choice of *how* a 0 hit point result is interpreted for a creature that is not at risk of death.

SRD Conditions – Unconscious

> An unconscious creature is incapacitated, can’t move or speak, and is unaware of its surroundings.

And

> The creature is stable if it has 0 hit points and is not making death saving throws. An unconscious creature that is stable regains 1 hit point after 1d4 hours.

A creature that is reduced to 0 hit points by a melee attack is therefore unconscious and incapacitated, and it remains so until its hit points are restored. The unconscious condition, and the incapacitated condition that comes with it, ends the moment the creature regains any hit points, e.g. 1 hit point from natural healing, magical healing, or otherwise. If the creature is not killed outright the unconscious state will persist, in the stable case, until it regains hit points after 1d4 hours, and it can be kept incapacitated by being kept at 0 hit points and stable.

The SRD does not give a general “deal non-lethal damage” attack mode. The DMG contains a variant rule for non-lethal damage, but that is a variant, not a core general rule. Within core rules the only thing the rules give you is the normal consequence of dropping a creature to 0 hit points: it becomes unconscious, and that unconsciousness lasts until the creature regains hit points.

answers.candidate_answer:
In the SRD 5.2.1 the saving throw procedure is mechanical, not a decision.

A saving throw is defined as:

*“When you make a saving throw, you roll a d20 and add the appropriate ability modifier. Some saving throws also add your proficiency bonus.”* SRD 5.2.1 Saving Throws

The DC is set by the effect and the roll is made against that DC:

*“If the d20 roll + the modifier is equal to or higher than the DC, the saving throw is a success.”* SRD 5.2.1 Saving Throws

Willingness is not a mechanic that changes the resolution of a saving throw. A creature is either a target of an effect that calls for a save, or it is not. Once it is a target the rules call for a d20 roll + the relevant ability modifier [+ proficiency if proficient] to be compared to the DC. There is no general rule in the SRD that allows a creature to voluntarily succeed or voluntarily fail a saving throw, to take a penalty to the roll, or to forgo rolling.

“Willing” is a targeting condition used by some effects, e.g.:

*“A willing creature can…”* and spells that require a willing target. Willingness removes the usual objection to being targeted; it does not waive the saving throw that the effect prescribes, nor does it give the creature the ability to choose the outcome of the roll.

If the effect says *“make a Wisdom saving throw”* the character must make that saving throw in the normal way. If the character wants the effect to succeed they are wanting to fail the save, but the rules as written do not provide a voluntary failure option for saving throws. The roll is made and the result is applied as normal.

A voluntary success/failure option only exists where an effect specifically grants it. Absent such a specific exception the save is resolved normally.

*Savage Attacker.* When you roll damage for a melee weapon with which you are proficient, you can reroll the damage dice and use either total. Once per turn.

The limitation is “Once per turn”, not once per attack, and not once per hit.

a) No. The feat is limited to one use per turn. The Attack action at Fighter 5 gives two attacks on the same turn. Even though both attacks hit and both are made with a melee weapon with which you are proficient, the feat can be used only once on that turn. You may choose to apply the one allowed reroll to either of the two hits, or to neither. In particular you may see the result of the first hit’s damage, decide not to use the feat on it, and then use the one-per-turn reroll on the second hit’s damage. The once-per-turn limit is only that you cannot use it more than once on the turn, not that you must use it on the first eligible roll.

c) Yes. The once-per-turn limit resets on a new turn. On the next turn the single Longsword attack is a new qualifying melee weapon damage roll made on a new turn. You may reroll the damage dice for that hit and use either total, subject to the normal once-per-turn limit for that turn.

Under SRD 5.2.1 an Opportunity Attack is not automatic on leaving reach.

* Making an Opportunity Attack. You can make an Opportunity Attack when a creature that you can see leaves your reach. To make the attack, take a Reaction to make one melee attack with a weapon or an Unarmed Strike against that creature.

An Opportunity Attack is therefore provoked by a creature voluntarily leaving your reach, and the response is limited to

* one melee attack with a weapon or an Unarmed Strike,
* made with your Reaction, and
* only against a creature you can see.

Avoiding Opportunity Attacks. You can avoid provoking an Opportunity Attack by taking the Disengage action. You also don’t provoke an Opportunity Attack when you Teleport or when you are moved without using your movement, action, Bonus Action, or Reaction. For example, you don’t provoke an Opportunity Attack if an explosion hurls you out of a foe’s reach or if you fall past an enemy.

Application to the three movements:

* Wizard – Misty Step. Misty Step is teleportation. The rule expressly says “You also don’t provoke an Opportunity Attack when you Teleport”. The wizard’s 30 ft teleport leaves the ogre’s 5-ft reach with no Opportunity Attack, even though the ogre can see the wizard and has its Reaction available.

* Cleric – moved 10 ft away by the goblin shaman’s Thunderwave. The cleric is “moved without using your movement, action, Bonus Action, or Reaction.” The rule expressly says you don’t provoke an Opportunity Attack when you are moved without using your movement, action, Bonus Action, or Reaction. “For example, you don’t provoke an Opportunity Attack if an explosion hurls you out of a foe’s reach”. Thunderwave hurling the cleric is that case. No Opportunity Attack is possible against the cleric.

* Fighter – walks 20 ft away using her Speed. This is voluntary movement using the fighter’s own movement. It is not Teleport, it is not movement forced by another creature or effect, and the fighter has not taken the Disengage action. The fighter leaves the ogre’s 5-ft reach and can be seen. That is the normal provoking circumstance.

The ogre can therefore use its Reaction on the fighter’s turn to make one Opportunity Attack. The attack must be

* one melee attack,
* with a weapon the ogre is wielding or an Unarmed Strike,
* against the fighter.

The ogre may not make a ranged attack, may not make more than one attack, and may not use the attack against the wizard or the cleric because neither provoked.

*If you don’t want to resist the effect, you can choose to fail the save without rolling.*

A willing character who wants the effect to work is a character who does not want to resist the effect. The character is not forced to roll. The player may simply declare that the character fails the Wisdom saving throw, and no die is rolled. The result of the save is then resolved as written in the effect that called for it.

That is the only option the rules give. You cannot choose to succeed against your will, and you do not have to roll to fail.
